You host, feed, connect, secure and observe what runs around them: containers that serve a model-backed API, databases that hold documents and embeddings, queues and events that move work between components, and the secrets, configuration and telemetry that keep everything running. The audience profile asks for Azure and third-party SDKs, data services, messaging and eventing, vector databases, monitoring and troubleshooting, containers, and Python. That's why every code sample in this pack is Python.

lessons.title: 1.1 · Azure Container Registry and ACR Tasks
lessons.summary: Store, tag, lock and clean up images in a registry, pull them with Entra identities, and build images in Azure with quick tasks, triggers and multi-step tasks.

blocks.text:
A registry stores container images and other OCI artifacts. Images that share a name form a repository. Each image has a manifest, which lists its layers and is identified by a SHA-256 digest. A tag is a readable alias that points at one manifest, and one manifest can carry several tags or none.

The three SKUs, Basic, Standard and Premium, expose the same programmatic capabilities and data-plane APIs, and every SKU gets zone redundancy in regions that support it. They differ in included storage, throughput and limits (webhooks, for example, are capped at 2, 10 and 500). Standard and Premium add anonymous pull access and artifact cache rules. Only Premium offers geo-replication, private endpoints through Private Link, dedicated agent pools for tasks and the retention policy for untagged manifests. Moving down from Premium switches the Premium features off. A SKU change itself causes no downtime.
blocks.title: Registries, repositories and SKUs

blocks.text:
Two tagging styles serve two purposes:
• Stable tags (python:3.12, app:1) are reused on purpose. Publishers move them to a newer digest whenever they patch the image, so they suit the base images you build from.
• Unique tags (a build ID or the digest itself) are never reused. A Git commit hash is only semi-stable, because a base-image rebuild runs from the same commit. Deploy from these, so that a restart or a scale-out pulls exactly the build you tested.

Lock what you deploy. Setting write-enabled to false stops an image being overwritten or deleted, and delete-enabled false on its own blocks only deletion. You can lock by tag, by manifest digest (repo@sha256:...) or a whole repository. Tag and manifest attributes are separate: locking a tag doesn't lock its manifest.

Storage needs housekeeping. When a stable tag moves, the old manifest stays behind untagged, and its manifest and unique layers still occupy storage. Untagging alone frees nothing, so you delete such manifests by digest. Two automated options exist, and both are preview: the acr purge command, usually run as a scheduled ACR task, and the Premium retention policy. The retention policy covers only manifests that become untagged after you turn it on.
blocks.title: Tags, locks and clean-up

blocks.text:
ACR Tasks builds and runs containers inside Azure, so a build agent doesn't need a local Docker engine.
• Quick task: az acr build sends a build context (a local folder or a Git URL) to the registry, builds the Dockerfile there and, by default, pushes the result to the same registry.
• Triggered task: az acr task create defines a reusable task. Triggers start it on a commit (on by default) or a pull request (off by default) in GitHub or Azure DevOps, on a base image update, or on a timer schedule. A source trigger needs a personal access token so the task can install the repository webhook. Commit and pull request triggers don't work with GitHub Enterprise repositories.
• Multi-step task: a YAML file of build, cmd and push steps, so one task can build, test and then push. Run variables such as {{.Run.ID}} give every run a unique tag.

Base image triggers are on by default for a new task. The task must run once before it knows its dependencies, and it reacts only when the stable tag it builds from gets a new digest. A base image in an Azure registry triggers a run immediately. A public base image in Docker Hub or Microsoft Container Registry is checked at a random interval of 10 to 60 minutes. Only the final runtime image is tracked; build-stage images in a multi-stage Dockerfile aren't. Learn recommends copying public base images into your own registry and building from that copy.

At the time of writing, the overview page notes that task runs are temporarily paused for subscriptions on Azure free credits.
blocks.title: ACR Tasks

blocks.text:
# Quick task: build in Azure from the current folder, one unique tag per run
az acr build --registry myregistry --image orders-api:{{.Run.ID}} .

# Triggered task: commits to main rebuild the image (base image trigger is on too)
az acr task create --registry myregistry --name orders-ci \
  --image "orders-api:{{.Run.ID}}" \
  --context "$REPO_URL#main" --file Dockerfile \
  --git-access-token "$GIT_PAT"

# Lock the manifest that production runs (by digest, so can_delete shows it)
az acr repository update --name myregistry \
  --image "orders-api@$PROD_DIGEST" --write-enabled false

# Weekly clean-up task (acr purge is preview): old tags and untagged manifests
PURGE_CMD="acr purge --filter 'orders-api:.*' --ago 30d --untagged"
az acr task create --registry myregistry --name weekly-purge \
  --cmd "$PURGE_CMD" --schedule "0 3 * * Sun" --context /dev/null

version: v1.1.0
steps:
  - build: -t {{.Run.Registry}}/orders-api:{{.Run.ID}} -f Dockerfile .
  - cmd: {{.Run.Registry}}/orders-api:{{.Run.ID}} python -m pytest -q
  - push:
      - {{.Run.Registry}}/orders-api:{{.Run.ID}}

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.containerregistry import ArtifactManifestOrder, ContainerRegistryClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

KEEP = 15
endpoint = os.environ["ACR_ENDPOINT"]   # the registry login server with its scheme
audience = os.environ["ACR_AUDIENCE"]   # the Azure Resource Manager audience

with ContainerRegistryClient(endpoint, DefaultAzureCredential(),
                             audience=audience) as client:
    newest_first = client.list_manifest_properties(
        "orders-api", order_by=ArtifactManifestOrder.LAST_UPDATED_ON_DESCENDING)
    for position, manifest in enumerate(newest_first):
        if position < KEEP or not manifest.can_delete:
            continue  # recent builds and manifests locked by digest stay
        client.delete_manifest("orders-api", manifest.digest)
blocks.title: Python · prune_manifests.py (azure-containerregistry)

blocks.text:
• Building without Docker on the agent points to az acr build, a quick task.
• Geo-replication, private endpoints and dedicated task agent pools need Premium. Anonymous pull needs Standard or Premium.
• Deploy from unique tags; build from stable base tags. A base image trigger fires when the stable tag gets a new digest, not when a new version tag appears.
• Untagging frees no storage while the manifest remains. Delete by digest, purge or use the retention policy (both preview).
• A pull-only workload needs AcrPull, not a push or owner role.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: A team pushes app:latest from a laptop and patches the Python base image by hand. A security fix took weeks to reach production, and a rollback once pulled an unexpected build. The fix: copy the public base image into the team's registry, create a task with a commit trigger (the base image trigger comes on by default), tag every build with {{.Run.ID}}, deploy by that tag, lock released tags, and schedule a purge task for old tags. Because the base now lives in an Azure registry, a patched base starts a rebuild straight away instead of waiting for the next public poll.
blocks.title: Worked scenario

blocks.text: Question: in prune_manifests.py, why skip manifests whose can_delete is False instead of deleting them? Solution: those manifests are locked (delete-enabled false on the manifest), so a delete fails unless you first unlock them with update_manifest_properties, which is what the SDK's own clean-up sample does. The lock has to be on the manifest, set by digest: a lock on a tag doesn't change the manifest's can_delete.

lessons.title: 1.2 · Containers on Azure App Service: settings and secrets
lessons.summary: Run a custom container on App Service, pull it from Azure Container Registry with a managed identity, and supply environment variables and Key Vault secrets through app settings.

blocks.text:
App Service pulls your image, starts the container and sends HTTP traffic to it. It assumes the container listens on port 80. If your server listens on another port, set the WEBSITES_PORT app setting to that port number.

Pulling from a private registry works two ways. You can store registry credentials on the app. The better way is a managed identity: give the app's identity the AcrPull role on the registry and set the acrUseManagedIdentityCreds site property to true. For a user-assigned identity, also set acrUserManagedIdentityID to its client ID. The registry must accept Azure Resource Manager audience tokens (az acr config authentication-as-arm). If it doesn't, pulls fail with an UNAUTHORIZED token validation error.

The first start pulls every layer. Later restarts reuse the cached layers and pull only what changed. Logs from the Docker host are on by default. Container console output needs container logging switched on (az webapp log config --docker-container-logging filesystem), and az webapp log tail then streams it.

Multi-container apps built on Docker Compose retire on 31 March 2027. Sidecar containers replace them.
blocks.title: Running a custom container

blocks.text:
Every app setting is injected into the container process as an environment variable, so Python code just reads os.environ. Registry credentials saved on the app are the exception: they are reserved variables that the application never sees. Any configuration change restarts the app, so for a production app Learn suggests making the change in a staging slot first and swapping.

Secrets belong in Key Vault. Instead of the value, the app setting holds a Key Vault reference in one of two forms:
• @Microsoft.KeyVault(...) wrapping SecretUri=<secret URI>, optionally with a version at the end of the URI
• @Microsoft.KeyVault(...) wrapping VaultName=<vault>; SecretName=<name>, with an optional SecretVersion
The app resolves the reference with its system-assigned identity by default. To use a user-assigned identity instead, set keyVaultReferenceIdentity to its resource ID. That is also the way to go when a reference must resolve at creation time, before any system-assigned identity exists. With the Azure RBAC model, the identity needs the Key Vault Secrets User role.

Rotation and refresh: a reference without a version follows the latest version. App Service caches resolved values and refetches them every 24 hours. Any configuration change restarts the app and refetches at once, and an authenticated POST to the app's Key Vault references refresh endpoint (under config/configreferences in Resource Manager) forces resolution. Because each environment should have its own vault, mark settings that hold references as slot settings so they don't move during a swap.

When a reference can't be resolved, the app receives the literal @Microsoft.KeyVault(...) string. The usual causes are missing access, a deleted secret or a syntax error. The portal shows the resolution status when you edit the setting, and a diagnostics detector for Key Vault application settings (under Diagnose and solve problems) explains failures.
blocks.title: Settings become environment variables

blocks.text:
az webapp create --resource-group rg-app --plan plan-linux --name orders-web \
  --container-image-name myregistry.azurecr.io/orders-api:cd71

principal=$(az webapp identity assign -g rg-app -n orders-web \
  --query principalId -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee "$principal" --role AcrPull \
  --scope "$(az acr show -n myregistry --query id -o tsv)"
az webapp config set -g rg-app -n orders-web \
  --generic-configurations '{"acrUseManagedIdentityCreds": true}'

# The identity reads secret values through Key Vault RBAC
az role assignment create --assignee "$principal" --role "Key Vault Secrets User" \
  --scope "$(az keyvault show -n kv-orders --query id -o tsv)"

az webapp config appsettings set -g rg-app -n orders-web --settings \
  WEBSITES_PORT=5000 SEARCH_TOP_K=5 \
  WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE=true \
  "PAYMENT_KEY=@Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=kv-orders;SecretName=payment-key)"

blocks.text:

• Pulling without stored registry credentials: managed identity + AcrPull + acrUseManagedIdentityCreds (plus acrUserManagedIdentityID for a user-assigned identity).
• The identity reads values with Key Vault Secrets User.
• A rotated secret appears within 24 hours. Restart, change any setting or call the refresh endpoint to pick it up sooner. Put a version in the reference only when you don't want rotation to flow through.
• A reference must resolve while the app is being created: use a user-assigned identity and keyVaultReferenceIdentity.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: After a scheduled rotation, an app keeps calling a partner API with the previous key for most of a day. Its reference has no version, so it will pick up the new value, but only on the 24-hour refetch. To switch now, restart the app or call the refresh endpoint. To make it routine, add the refresh call to the rotation runbook.

Solution: persistent storage is off by default for Linux custom containers. Turn on the App Service storage app setting (shown in the CLI sample above), or mount an Azure Storage path. Anything written outside those locations never survives a restart.

lessons.title: 1.3 · Azure Container Apps: environments, revisions and KEDA scaling
lessons.summary: Deploy to a Container Apps environment, manage revisions and traffic, wire secrets and identities, and scale on events with KEDA-based rules.

blocks.text:
An environment is the secure boundary around a group of container apps and jobs. Apps in one environment share a virtual network and send their logs to the same Log Analytics workspace, and Dapr apps there can use service invocation and a shared Dapr configuration. Workload profiles environments are the default type and run both the serverless Consumption profile and Dedicated profiles. Consumption-only environments are the legacy type. An environment that stays idle, or stuck in a failed or blocked state, for more than 90 days is deleted automatically.

Every change to a container app is one of two kinds:
• Revision-scope changes are edits under properties.template, such as the image, container settings, environment variables and scale rules. Each one creates a new revision. Revisions are immutable snapshots.
• Application-scope changes are edits under properties.configuration, such as secret values, ingress (including traffic splitting rules), registries and Dapr settings. They apply to every revision and don't create a new one.
blocks.title: Environments and the two kinds of change

blocks.text:
• Single (the default): a new revision is provisioned and scaled up, and it must pass its startup and readiness probes. Only then does traffic move to it and the old revision is deactivated. Until that point the old revision keeps all the traffic, so a bad image causes no downtime.
• Multiple: several revisions stay active, you split traffic between them by weight, and you decide when old revisions are deprovisioned. The weights must add up to 100%. This mode is the basis for blue-green and canary releases. A revision suffix such as a commit hash gives revisions predictable names (app--suffix).
• Deployment labels (preview) are a third mode built on labels.
A label gives one revision its own stable URL. Moving the label to another revision switches that traffic without changing the URL, and labelled traffic doesn't need a weight. Container Apps keeps up to 100 inactive revisions by default. Changing that limit is a preview setting.
blocks.title: Revision modes, traffic and labels

blocks.text:
Secrets are defined at application level (configuration.secrets), so adding or changing one never creates a revision. An environment variable refers to a secret with secretref:<name>, and scale rules can refer to secrets too. A secret can instead be a Key Vault reference, keyvaultref:<secret URI>,identityref:<identity>, resolved by a managed identity that holds Key Vault Secrets User. A reference without a version picks up a new version within 30 minutes, and active revisions that use it in an environment variable restart automatically. For a plain secret value that you change yourself, running revisions keep using the old value. A revision restart, or a fresh revision, picks up the change.

To pull from Azure Container Registry without credentials, give the app a system-assigned or user-assigned identity that has AcrPull and pass it as the registry identity.
blocks.title: Secrets, identities and image pulls

blocks.text:
Each revision scales between a minimum and a maximum replica count (defaults 0 and 10, configurable up to 1,000). Rules are HTTP (concurrent requests, default threshold 10), TCP (concurrent connections) or custom. A custom rule accepts any KEDA ScaledObject scaler, such as azure-servicebus. You copy the scaler's type and metadata from the KEDA specification into the rule. Scaler authentication uses a Container Apps secret, or a managed identity when the source is an Azure Storage queue, Service Bus or Event Hubs. The portal can't configure managed identity for scale rules, so use the CLI, ARM or Bicep.

How custom rules behave:
• KEDA polls the source every 30 seconds and computes desiredReplicas = ceil(metric ÷ target), capped by the maximum.
• Scale-out goes in steps of 1, 4, 8, 16 and so on, with no scale-up stabilization window.
• Scale-in waits for a 300-second stabilization window. The 300-second cooldown applies only to the last step, from one replica to zero.
• An app with ingress disabled, no custom rule and a minimum of 0 scales to zero and has nothing to wake it again. Give it a rule or a minimum of at least 1.
blocks.title: Scaling with KEDA

blocks.text:
az containerapp create -g rg-app -n orders-worker --environment cae-orders \
  --image myregistry.azurecr.io/orders-worker:cd71 \
  --user-assigned "$UAMI_ID" \
  --registry-server myregistry.azurecr.io --registry-identity "$UAMI_ID" \
  --secrets "pay-key=keyvaultref:$PAY_KEY_URI,identityref:$UAMI_ID" \
  --env-vars "PAYMENT_KEY=secretref:pay-key" "AZURE_CLIENT_ID=$UAMI_CLIENT_ID" \
  --min-replicas 0 --max-replicas 15 \
  --scale-rule-name orders-queue --scale-rule-type azure-servicebus \
  --scale-rule-metadata "queueName=orders" "namespace=sb-orders" \
    "messageCount=20" \
  --scale-rule-identity "$UAMI_ID"

az containerapp update -g rg-app -n orders-api \
  --image myregistry.azurecr.io/orders-api:e9f2 --revision-suffix e9f2
az containerapp ingress traffic set -g rg-app -n orders-api \
  --revision-weight orders-api--cd71=80 orders-api--e9f2=20

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import ServiceBusClient

# With only a user-assigned identity, Azure Identity needs its client ID:
# AZURE_CLIENT_ID (set in the create command) tells DefaultAzureCredential.
credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
with ServiceBusClient(os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"], credential) as client:
    with client.get_queue_receiver("orders", max_wait_time=30) as receiver:
        for message in receiver:
            print("handling", message.message_id)
            receiver.complete_message(message)
blocks.title: Python · worker.py (drains the queue the rule watches)

blocks.text:
• Image, environment variables and scale rules create revisions. Secrets, ingress and traffic weights don't.
• Splitting traffic by weight needs multiple revision mode, and the weights must total 100.
• With messageCount 20 and 130 messages waiting, the target is ceil(130 ÷ 20) = 7 replicas. From one replica KEDA steps to 4, then 7.
• The 300-second cooldown is for the final scale-in to zero only.
• A worker without ingress needs a custom rule or a minimum replica count of at least 1.
• Managed identity on a scale rule: CLI, ARM or Bicep, not the portal.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: A batch worker should cost nothing while idle but keep up when an upstream system drops thousands of orders into a queue. It runs without ingress, scales from 0 to 15 replicas on an azure-servicebus custom rule, and authenticates the rule with a user-assigned identity that has access to the namespace. The same identity has AcrPull for image pulls and Key Vault Secrets User for the payment key reference. One identity, created before the app, serves all three needs.
blocks.title: Worked scenario

blocks.text: Question: in single revision mode, a new revision is created but traffic stays on the old one. What must the new revision do before traffic moves? Solution: provision successfully, scale up to the previous revision's replica count (within its own minimum and maximum), and have every replica pass its startup and readiness probes. Until then the old revision keeps all the traffic.

lessons.title: 1.4 · AKS manifests and troubleshooting AKS and Container Apps
lessons.summary: Deploy to AKS with manifest files, expose pods with Services, and diagnose failing pods, revisions and connections with logs, events and connectivity checks.

blocks.text:
AKS runs Kubernetes with a managed control plane and comes in two cluster modes, AKS Automatic and AKS Standard. You describe the desired state in YAML manifest files and apply them with kubectl apply -f <file>, and Kubernetes works to make the cluster match.
• A Deployment declares the replica count, a label selector and a pod template: containers, images, ports, environment, resources and probes. Learn recommends at least two replicas for resilience.
• Resource requests and limits: set CPU and memory limits for every pod so one workload can't exhaust a node. A container that goes over its memory limit is killed (OOMKilled).
• Probes: the kubelet uses a readiness probe to decide whether a pod receives traffic (a pod that isn't ready leaves the Service's endpoints), a liveness probe to decide when to restart a container, and a startup probe to hold the other two back until a slow starter is up.
• A Pod Disruption Budget keeps a minimum number of pods running during voluntary disruptions such as upgrades.
• A Service gives the selected pods a stable address. ClusterIP (the default) is internal only, NodePort maps a port on each node, LoadBalancer creates an Azure load balancer with an external IP, and ExternalName maps to a DNS name. A new LoadBalancer Service shows EXTERNAL-IP as <pending> until the address is assigned.

To pull from Azure Container Registry, attach the registry (az aks update --attach-acr). That grants AcrPull to the cluster's kubelet identity. Attaching isn't supported for registries that use the ABAC repository permissions mode.

Work from the outside in:
• kubectl get pods shows STATUS and RESTARTS. CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps exiting with a non-zero code. Typical causes are bad configuration, missing environment variables or ConfigMaps, a too-low limit or a misconfigured probe. ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull means the image can't be pulled. Exit code 137 with reason OOMKilled means the memory limit was exceeded.
• kubectl describe pod <pod> ends with the pod's events. They explain image pull and probe failures and other warnings. kubectl get events lists events cluster-wide, but Kubernetes keeps events for one hour only, so export them if you need history.
• kubectl logs <pod> shows output, and -c <container> picks a container. For a container that keeps restarting, kubectl logs <pod> --previous shows the last run before the crash.
• Connectivity: curl the pod IP from a test pod, then the Service IP. kubectl describe service shows the selector and endpoints, and kubectl get endpoints lists the pods behind it. An empty endpoint list means no ready pod matches the selector. Check network policies too. az aks check-acr tests whether the cluster can reach a registry.

blocks.text:
Container Apps separates two log streams:
• Console logs are what your container writes to stdout and stderr.
• System logs come from the platform: revision provisioning (including image pull, timeout and crash errors), traffic weights, Dapr components, volume mounts and authentication.
Stream either one with az containerapp logs show --type console or --type system, adding --follow for a live stream or --tail for the last messages. In Log Analytics the tables are ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL and ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL, with columns such as ContainerAppName_s, RevisionName_s and Log_s.

Common symptoms and what to check:
• A new revision fails to deploy: check that the app can pull its image.
• A revision stays Provisioning, or becomes Degraded: check the health probes. TCP probes must use the same port as the ingress target port.
• Requests fail: check that ingress is enabled, that external traffic is allowed (an internal-only setting rejects other callers) and that the target port is the port the app listens on.
• Responses come from the wrong version: check traffic weights and deploy with unique image tags.
• The log stream reports that the revision is scaled to zero: run it with a minimum of one replica while you debug.
az containerapp revision list shows each revision's health, and az containerapp replica list shows its replicas.

lessons.title: 2.1 · Cosmos DB for NoSQL: SDK, queries, RUs, indexing and consistency
lessons.summary: Connect with the Python SDK and Microsoft Entra ID, prefer point reads and single-partition queries, read the RU charge, and tune indexing policies and consistency levels.

blocks.text:
The azure-cosmos package gives you CosmosClient, then a database client, then a container client. Create one CosmosClient and reuse it for the life of the process. The Python client is thread-safe and handles connections efficiently, so one shared instance is the recommended pattern. In Python every request goes via the Cosmos DB gateway: the Python SDK offers no Direct connectivity.

Sign in with Microsoft Entra ID: pass a DefaultAzureCredential to CosmosClient and give the identity a data-plane role, either Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader or Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor, assigned with az cosmosdb sql role assignment create. Data-plane roles read and write data but don't manage resources such as databases and containers. Create those through the control plane, with Bicep, ARM or the CLI.
blocks.title: Connecting from Python

blocks.text:
Every operation is charged in Request Units (RUs), a single currency that covers CPU, IOPS and memory. You pay for RUs in one of three modes: provisioned throughput (RU/s set in steps of 100), autoscale, or serverless.
• Point reads (read_item with the id and the partition key value) cost fewer RUs than queries. Use one whenever you know both values.
• Queries: query_items with parameters, never values pasted into the SQL text. When you pass partition_key, the query stays in one partition and the SDK skips a query-plan call to the gateway. A query without the partition key fans out to all physical partitions, so it gets slower and costlier as the container grows. max_item_count sets the page size.
• Writes: upsert_item, create_item, replace_item and delete_item. Bigger items and more indexed properties both raise the write charge.
The charge for the last call is in the x-ms-request-charge response header (read last_response_headers on container.client_connection). For a query, set populate_query_metrics=True for execution metrics and populate_index_metrics=True to see which indexes were used and which ones Cosmos DB recommends.
blocks.title: Operations and what they cost

blocks.text:
By default every property of every item is indexed, with indexing mode consistent, which means the index is updated synchronously with each write. That makes any filter cheap to query but makes every write pay for every path. Tune the policy:
• Keep the root path /* included and exclude the paths you never filter or sort on, such as long text or large arrays. This is the recommended strategy, because new properties still get indexed. The alternative excludes /* and includes only the listed paths. In that case remember to include the partition key path.
• When an included path and an excluded path conflict, the more precise path wins.
• Sorting on several properties at once (ORDER BY a, b) requires a composite index whose paths follow the same order. Composite indexes also help some combinations of filter and sort.
• Indexing mode none turns indexing off for a pure key-value container.
id and _ts are always indexed in consistent mode, and _etag is excluded by default.
blocks.title: Indexing policies

blocks.text:
From strongest to weakest: Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix, Eventual. You set a default on the account and can override it for reads, per client or per request. Strong and Bounded staleness need two replicas for every read (a minority quorum), while the other three levels use one, so for the same RUs the two strong levels give half the read throughput. Write throughput is the same at every level.

Session is the most widely used level. Within a session, a client reads its own writes because the SDK keeps a session token for each partition and sends it with reads. A brand-new client has no tokens yet, so until it writes it reads like Eventual. After you change the account default, restart the applications so their clients pick up the new level.
blocks.title: Consistency levels

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

# One client per process, reused everywhere
credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
client = CosmosClient(os.environ["COSMOS_ENDPOINT"], credential=credential)
orders = client.get_database_client("shop").get_container_client("orders")

# Point read: id plus partition key value
order = orders.read_item(item="ord-1009", partition_key="cust-42")

# Parameterized single-partition query
rows = list(orders.query_items(
    query="SELECT c.id, c.total FROM c WHERE c.status = @status",
    parameters=[{"name": "@status", "value": "open"}],
    partition_key="cust-42",
    populate_index_metrics=True,
))
headers = orders.client_connection.last_response_headers
print("RU charge:", headers["x-ms-request-charge"])

blocks.text:
• You know the id and the partition key: read_item, not a SELECT on c.id.
• ORDER BY on two properties needs a composite index in the same order.
• Writes cost too much and most properties are never filtered: exclude them from the index.
• Read-your-writes for one user at low cost: Session. Strong and Bounded staleness halve read throughput for the same RUs.
• Entra data-plane roles can't create databases or containers. Use the control plane.
• Python can't switch to Direct mode. It always uses Gateway.

blocks.text: An order history page runs a query without a partition key and sorts by two fields, and every call is slow and expensive. Two fixes: pass the customer's partition key so the query stays in one partition and skips the query-plan call, and add a composite index that matches the ORDER BY. The x-ms-request-charge header before and after each change shows what each fix saved.

lessons.title: 2.2 · Cosmos DB vector search and the change feed
lessons.summary: Define a vector embedding policy and a vector index, run VectorDistance queries for semantic retrieval, and react to new or updated items through the change feed.

blocks.text:
Store each chunk's embedding as an array property next to its text and metadata, so one query can filter and rank. Vector indexing and search are on by default, with no feature to register or account capability to enable. A container needs two settings:
• A vector embedding policy that lists each vector path with its dataType (float32, float16, int8 or uint8), its dimensions and its distanceFunction (cosine, the default, or dotproduct or euclidean). float16 halves the storage that float32 needs, at some cost in accuracy.
• An entry under vectorIndexes in the indexing policy for the same path. Learn's examples also list that path under excludedPaths so the regular index skips it.

Once vector indexing and search are enabled on a container, they can't be turned off. Accounts with shared throughput don't support them.
blocks.title: Vectors in Cosmos DB for NoSQL

blocks.text: Both quantized types (quantizedFlat, diskANN) only take effect once 1,000 or more vectors are indexed. Below that, a query runs a full scan and can cost more RUs.
blocks.title: Vector index types
rows: 100% recall; stored with the other indexes
fast at scale; results can vary between runs

blocks.text: VectorDistance(c.embedding, @queryVector) scores each item, and ORDER BY VectorDistance(...) puts the nearest first. Always add TOP N, because without it the query tries to return far more results and costs more RUs and latency. Without ORDER BY, TOP N returns arbitrary items rather than the closest. Pass the query vector and N as parameters. Add WHERE filters on tenant, type or date, and pass partition_key, so the search stays narrow. For diskANN you can raise searchListSizeMultiplier in VectorDistance's options to trade latency for recall on a single query.
blocks.title: Querying

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient, PartitionKey
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
client = CosmosClient(os.environ["COSMOS_ENDPOINT"], credential=credential)
db = client.get_database_client("kb")

embedding_policy = {"vectorEmbeddings": [{
    "path": "/embedding", "dataType": "float32",
    "distanceFunction": "cosine", "dimensions": 1536}]}
indexing_policy = {
    "includedPaths": [{"path": "/*"}],
    "excludedPaths": [{"path": "/embedding/*"}],
    "vectorIndexes": [{"path": "/embedding", "type": "diskANN"}],
}
# Creating containers is a control-plane operation: use an identity allowed to
# manage resources here, or create the container with Bicep or the CLI instead.
chunks = db.create_container_if_not_exists(
    id="chunks", partition_key=PartitionKey(path="/ownerId"),
    indexing_policy=indexing_policy, vector_embedding_policy=embedding_policy)


def nearest(query_vector, owner, k=5):
    sql = ("SELECT TOP @k c.id, c.text, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @v) AS similarity "
           "FROM c WHERE c.ownerId = @o ORDER BY VectorDistance(c.embedding, @v)")
    return list(chunks.query_items(
        query=sql,
        parameters=[{"name": "@k", "value": k}, {"name": "@v", "value": query_vector},
                    {"name": "@o", "value": owner}],
        partition_key=owner))
blocks.title: Python · cosmos_vectors.py

blocks.text:
The change feed is a persistent record of changes to a container. It has two modes:
• Latest version (the default) records creates and updates and gives you the current version of each changed item. Intermediate versions can be skipped, and deletes aren't recorded. To see deletions, write a soft-delete flag instead of deleting. You can start from the beginning of the container, from a point in time, from now or from a saved checkpoint.
• All versions and deletes (preview) records every create, update and delete in order, including deletes caused by TTL expiry, with metadata that tells you which operation happened. It needs continuous backup, and you turn it on in the account's Features page. It can start only from now or from a checkpoint inside the backup retention window.

Ways to consume it from Python:
• The change feed processor library is for .NET and Java only. Python and Node.js use the pull model instead.
• Pull model: query_items_change_feed with start_time="Beginning", or mode="AllVersionsAndDeletes" (preview; needs azure-cosmos 4.9.1b1 or later), optionally with partition_key or a feed_range (read_feed_ranges returns one per physical partition) so that several workers can split the work. You save the continuation token yourself (the etag response header) and resume with continuation=.
• Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger: the platform manages the reading and keeps its state in a lease container, which the trigger can create for you (see the create option in the sample below). For Python functions the trigger uses latest version mode. If several functions watch the same container, give each one its own lease container or its own lease_container_prefix.
blocks.title: The change feed
Python · function_app.py (Cosmos DB trigger, v2 model)

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
client = CosmosClient(os.environ["COSMOS_ENDPOINT"], credential=credential)
articles = client.get_database_client("kb").get_container_client("articles")


def read_changes(saved_token=None):
    if saved_token:
        feed = articles.query_items_change_feed(continuation=saved_token)
    else:
        feed = articles.query_items_change_feed(start_time="Beginning")
    for item in feed:
        print("changed:", item["id"])
    # Persist this after the batch succeeds; pass it back next time.
    return articles.client_connection.last_response_headers["etag"]

blocks.text:
• More than 505 dimensions rules out flat. quantizedFlat and diskANN go to 4,096 and need 1,000 vectors before they help.
• A vector query needs TOP N and ORDER BY VectorDistance. Without ORDER BY you get arbitrary items.
• Latest version mode doesn't record deletes. Use a soft-delete flag, or all versions and deletes mode (preview, continuous backup required).
• The change feed processor library exists for .NET and Java only. Check which consumption options a language really has before you design around one.
• Two functions on one container with the same leases share the work instead of each seeing every change. Use separate lease containers or prefixes.

blocks.text: One worker can't keep up with the change feed of a large container. The team calls read_feed_ranges, which returns one feed range per physical partition, and gives each worker its own range through query_items_change_feed with feed_range set. Every worker keeps its own continuation token, so the ranges progress independently and the work spreads across machines.

lessons.title: 2.3 · Azure Database for PostgreSQL: connections, schema and pooling
lessons.summary: Connect from Python with Microsoft Entra ID, design tables that hold text and embeddings, and optimize connections with application pools and the built-in PgBouncer.

blocks.text:
This pack targets Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server. It speaks standard PostgreSQL, so Python uses an ordinary driver. The Learn quickstart uses psycopg (version 3, psycopg.connect) and connects over TLS with sslmode=require.

Passwordless sign-in with Microsoft Entra ID is the recommended option. The app gets an access token with DefaultAzureCredential for the PostgreSQL token scope (the ossrdbms-aad host under database.windows.net, ending in /.default) and sends that token as the password. The user name is the database role mapped to the Entra principal. A Microsoft Entra administrator, which can be a user, a group, a service principal or a managed identity, has the same privileges as the PostgreSQL administrator and can manage both Entra roles and local password roles. You can turn password authentication off completely. Tokens expire, so production code needs a refresh strategy: get a fresh token whenever a new physical connection opens, never once at startup.
blocks.title: Connect from Python

blocks.text:
import os

import psycopg
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from psycopg_pool import ConnectionPool

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
SCOPE = os.environ["PG_ENTRA_SCOPE"]  # the ossrdbms-aad .default scope


class EntraConnection(psycopg.Connection):
    @classmethod
    def connect(cls, conninfo="", **kwargs):
        kwargs["password"] = credential.get_token(SCOPE).token
        return super().connect(conninfo, **kwargs)


conninfo = (f"host={os.environ['PGHOST']} port=6432 dbname=kb "
            f"user={os.environ['PGUSER']} sslmode=require")
pool = ConnectionPool(conninfo, connection_class=EntraConnection,
                      min_size=1, max_size=5, open=True)

with pool.connection() as conn:
    rows = conn.execute(
        "SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE tenant = %s LIMIT 20", ("t-17",)
    ).fetchall()
blocks.title: Python · pg_pool.py (Entra token for each new connection)

blocks.text:
Keep source documents and their chunks in separate tables. A document has many chunks, and each chunk holds its text, the metadata you filter on and its embedding.
• The embedding column is the pgvector vector(n) type, with n equal to the model's output size (1,536 for text-embedding-ada-002). A vector column needs fixed dimensions, and ivfflat and hnsw can index at most 2,000 of them. For larger embeddings, use half-precision vectors (halfvec) or half-precision indexing, which reach 4,000 dimensions, or reduce the dimensions.
• The extension is called vector, not pgvector. Allow-list it in the azure.extensions server parameter (check with SHOW azure.extensions), then run CREATE EXTENSION vector in each database that needs it.
• Plain columns: Learn's own examples use bigint or bigserial keys and text for the content.
• Put metadata that queries filter on (tenant, category, date) into ordinary columns, so you can index it with B-tree, write partial indexes for common predicates (WHERE tier = 'premium'), or partition the table, for example by a date range or by tenant.
Load data in bulk with COPY, and upsert with INSERT … ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE.
blocks.title: Model the schema

blocks.text:
-- After 'vector' is allow-listed in azure.extensions
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE articles (
    id        bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant    text NOT NULL,
    title     text NOT NULL,
    category  text NOT NULL,
    published date NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE chunks (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    article_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES articles(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    tenant     text NOT NULL,
    chunk_no   int  NOT NULL,
    content    text NOT NULL,
    embedding  vector(1536) NOT NULL,
    UNIQUE (article_id, chunk_no)
);

CREATE INDEX chunks_tenant ON chunks (tenant);   -- B-tree for the filter column
blocks.title: SQL · schema.sql

blocks.text:
Opening a PostgreSQL connection is expensive, and every connection uses server memory. Code that connects per request, or a scale-out that multiplies the number of instances, can run into max_connections. Its default depends on the compute SKU, and changing it needs a server restart. Learn advises against raising it and recommends PgBouncer instead.
• Pool connections: Learn's pooling guidance is to keep a cache of connections and hand them out again instead of opening a new one per request. The sample above does this inside each process with psycopg_pool.
• Pool at the server: the built-in PgBouncer listens on port 6432 at the same host name (direct connections use 5432) and supports Microsoft Entra authentication. Its pool mode defaults to transaction, with default_pool_size 50 and max_client_conn 5,000, and it can multiplex up to 10,000 client connections. You switch it on with the pgbouncer.enabled server parameter, and no restart is needed.
• Limits: there's no PgBouncer on the Burstable tier. Moving a server from General Purpose or Memory Optimized to Burstable loses it. A restart, scale operation or failover restarts PgBouncer, so clients must reconnect. In transaction mode, protocol-level prepared statements need the PgBouncer max_prepared_statements parameter set above 0.
The three pool modes are session (one server connection for the whole client session), transaction (one connection for each transaction) and statement (one connection for each statement).
blocks.title: Optimize connections

blocks.text:
• A Microsoft Entra administrator can be a group, which makes administration easier to share.
• Built-in PgBouncer: port 6432, transaction pool mode by default, no restart to switch it on, and a restart of the server restarts it too.
• PgBouncer isn't available on Burstable.
• vector(n) needs fixed dimensions. ivfflat and hnsw stop at 2,000 dimensions, halfvec indexing goes to 4,000.
• CREATE EXTENSION vector fails until vector is allow-listed in azure.extensions.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: After an app moves its connections to PgBouncer on port 6432, the queries that rely on protocol-level prepared statements start failing. PgBouncer runs in transaction mode by default, and it tracks named prepared statements only when its max_prepared_statements parameter is set above 0, which is off by default. Setting it fixes the errors. Statement pool mode can't be used with prepared statements at all.

lessons.summary: Choose and tune IVFFlat, HNSW and DiskANN indexes, cut vector compute overhead, size compute and storage, and run filtered semantic retrieval for a RAG pipeline.

blocks.text:
pgvector compares vectors with three distance operators: <-> (Euclidean, L2), <=> (cosine distance) and <#> (negative inner product). An index serves a query only when it was built with the matching operator class: vector_l2_ops for <->, vector_cosine_ops for <=>, vector_ip_ops for <#>. A nearest-neighbour query orders by the distance expression and ends with LIMIT. For vectors normalized to length 1, such as OpenAI embeddings, Learn suggests inner product for best performance.

Without a vector index the search is exact but reads every row (a sequential scan, possibly in parallel). Approximate indexes trade some recall for speed.
blocks.title: Operators and operator classes

blocks.text: ivfflat and hnsw index at most 2,000 dimensions. DiskANN product quantization (pg_diskann 0.6 and later) is preview, and so is its support for up to 16,000 dimensions.

rows: fast, little memory; needs a training step on existing rows
lists at build; ivfflat.probes at query time (default 1)
start with lists = rows/1000 (up to 1M rows) and probes = lists/10
slower and more memory; no training, can be built on an empty table
graph index built for very large sets
flexible server feature; install with CREATE EXTENSION pg_diskann CASCADE

blocks.text:
• Read the plan first: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, VERBOSE, BUFFERS) shows whether your index or a sequential scan answers the query, and whether the query ran in parallel. A mismatched operator class or a missing ORDER BY … LIMIT keeps the index out of the plan.
• Tune per query, not per server: SET LOCAL ivfflat.probes, hnsw.ef_search or diskann.l_value_is inside a transaction changes only that transaction. Higher values give better recall but cost more latency and CPU.
• Builds take memory. Raise maintenance_work_mem for the build session and watch pg_stat_progress_create_index.
• Fewer dimensions mean less work. Reduce dimensions, or use half-precision vectors, which also extend indexing to 4,000 dimensions.
• Filters are the classic trap. An approximate index scan runs first and the WHERE clause filters its candidates afterwards, so a selective filter can leave fewer rows than LIMIT asked for. With HNSW and ef_search at 40, a filter that matches 10% of rows leaves about 4 rows. Remedies: a B-tree index on the filter column for exact search when the filter matches few rows, partial indexes that repeat the query's exact predicate, partitioning (list partitioning by tenant works well), a higher ef_search, or, for DiskANN, its iterative search (diskann.iterative_search, relaxed_order by default).
blocks.title: Cutting vector compute overhead

blocks.text:
• Burstable runs on CPU credits. It suits workloads that are idle or below baseline most of the time and isn't meant for production. When the credits run out, the server can become unreachable, and it gets no built-in PgBouncer.
• General Purpose has 4 GiB of memory per vCore and suits most production workloads.
• Memory Optimized has 6.75 to 9.5 GiB per vCore. Choose it when vector indexes and hot data must stay in memory.
You can change vCores up or down after creation, but storage only grows. Premium SSD disks go up to 32,767 GiB. Premium SSD v2 has no fixed sizes and goes up to 64 TiB (65,536 GiB). Premium SSD v2 lets you set capacity, IOPS and throughput separately and reaches higher maximums (80,000 IOPS and 1,200 MB/s). Storage autogrow is GA for Premium SSD and preview for Premium SSD v2. A server switches to read-only mode when storage use reaches 95 percent, so autogrow and alerts matter for a growing corpus.
blocks.title: Compute, memory and storage
SQL · index, tune and check

blocks.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a model's answer in your data in three steps. Retrieve: query an index or data store for the content most relevant to the question. Augment: combine the question and that grounding data into a prompt. Generate: the model answers from the supplied content, which reduces guessing and lets the answer cite its sources. In PostgreSQL, the retrieve step is a vector query with ordinary WHERE clauses for the metadata (tenant, category, date) that limit it to rows the user may see.

Embeddings can come from your application or from the database. The azure_ai extension's azure_openai.create_embeddings function takes a deployment name and text and calls an Azure OpenAI deployment from SQL, after you store the endpoint and key with azure_ai.set_setting, or use a system-assigned managed identity instead of the key. The extension's AI functions, including embedding generation, are labelled preview.
blocks.title: RAG with metadata filters

blocks.text:
import numpy as np
import psycopg
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

SQL = """
SELECT c.content, a.title
FROM chunks c JOIN articles a ON a.id = c.article_id
WHERE c.tenant = %(tenant)s AND a.category = ANY(%(cats)s)
ORDER BY c.embedding <=> %(q)s
LIMIT %(k)s
"""


def retrieve(conn: psycopg.Connection, query_vec, tenant, cats, k=5):
    register_vector(conn)  # lets psycopg send numpy arrays as vector values
    params = {"q": np.asarray(query_vec, dtype=np.float32), "tenant": tenant,
              "cats": cats, "k": k}
    return conn.execute(SQL, params).fetchall()


def grounded_prompt(question, rows):
    sources = "\n".join(f"[{i}] {title}: {text}"
                        for i, (text, title) in enumerate(rows, 1))
    return ("Answer only from the numbered sources and cite them as [n]. "
            "If they don't contain the answer, say so.\n\n"
            f"{sources}\n\nQuestion: {question}")

• Cosine search with <=> needs an index built with vector_cosine_ops.
• ivfflat needs rows to train on, so build it after loading. hnsw and diskann can be created on an empty table.
• Higher probes, ef_search or l_value_is mean better recall but more latency and CPU. Set them with SET LOCAL for the queries that need them.
• A filtered query returns fewer rows than LIMIT: the filter ran after the approximate scan. Add a B-tree on the filter column, partial indexes or partitions, or raise the search list.
• More than 2,000 dimensions: halfvec (up to 4,000), or DiskANN with product quantization (preview).
• azure_ai embedding generation is preview.

blocks.text: Nearly every query on a growing chunks table asks only for documents published in the current year, yet each one searches the whole table. The team partitions the table by a range on the publication date, one partition per year, and checks in EXPLAIN that partitions which can't match are pruned. Queries for this year now touch one partition and its smaller vector index.

blocks.text: Question: a service runs SET hnsw.ef_search = 200 on a pooled connection for one report, and afterwards every query that reuses that connection is slower. Why? Solution: a plain SET lasts for the whole connection. Use SET LOCAL inside a transaction block, so the higher value applies only to that transaction's queries.

lessons.title: 2.5 · Azure Managed Redis: caching, expiration, invalidation and vector search
lessons.summary: Use Azure Managed Redis as a cache-aside layer with expiration and invalidation, and as a vector index for similarity search and semantic caching.

blocks.text:
Azure Managed Redis is the current service, built on Redis Enterprise software. Azure Cache for Redis is retiring: its Basic, Standard and Premium tiers on 30 September 2028, and its Enterprise and Enterprise Flash tiers on 31 March 2027. The tiers are Memory Optimized (8:1 memory to vCPU), Balanced (4:1), Compute Optimized (2:1) and Flash Optimized, which moves less-used data from RAM to NVMe storage. Some large SKUs are preview.

Clients connect over TLS on port 10000 (Azure Cache for Redis used 6380). New caches have Microsoft Entra ID enabled and access keys disabled, and Learn recommends Entra ID with managed identities.

Settle these at creation:
• Clustering policy. OSS is the default and the fastest, but the client must speak the Redis Cluster API, and it doesn't support RediSearch. Enterprise gives a single endpoint and supports RediSearch. Non-clustered is preview, available only for caches up to 25 GB, and also listed as RediSearch-capable on the architecture and quickstart pages. OSS and Enterprise can't be changed in place.
• Modules (Redis 7.4). RediSearch, RedisJSON, RedisBloom and RedisTimeSeries must be selected when you create the cache and can't be added later. Flash Optimized supports only RedisJSON. Redis 8.2, which includes every module, is preview.
• For vector search, Learn's pages differ. The Well-Architected guide says RediSearch requires the Enterprise clustering policy and the NoEviction eviction policy; the architecture and quickstart pages also allow the preview Non-clustered policy. The GA path is Enterprise with NoEviction.
blocks.title: The service and the choices you make at creation

blocks.text:
Cache-aside: read the key, and on a miss load from the data store, write the value to the cache and return it. The pattern suits caches that don't provide read-through or write-through themselves, so your code does the loading. Keep the cache consistent on writes in one of two ways:
• Invalidate on write: update the store, then delete the key, and the next read repopulates it. The write path stays simple, but a reader may briefly miss or see old data.
• Write-through: update the store and the cache in the same operation. Readers see the new value straight away, at the cost of more work on every write. Use it only for read-heavy paths that need read-after-write freshness.
Cache-aside never guarantees consistency. Another process can change the store at any moment, so pair it with expiration.

Expiration and memory: set a TTL on cached keys (SET with EX, or EXPIRE). Expiration removes keys proactively instead of waiting for memory pressure. Too short a TTL wastes the cache, and too long a TTL serves stale data and fills memory. The default eviction policy on Azure Managed Redis is volatile-lru, which evicts only keys that have a TTL, so a cache full of keys without TTLs evicts nothing. Each key also carries per-key overhead, and TTL bookkeeping adds a little more.

For shared data that several instances update, choose an approach to concurrency: optimistic (check that the value hasn't changed before you write) or pessimistic (lock while you update).
blocks.title: Caching, expiration and invalidation

blocks.text:
import json
import os

import redis
from redis_entraid.cred_provider import create_from_default_azure_credential

# REDIS_SCOPE holds the Azure Managed Redis .default token scope
provider = create_from_default_azure_credential((os.environ["REDIS_SCOPE"],))
r = redis.Redis(host=os.environ["REDIS_HOST"], port=10000, ssl=True,
                credential_provider=provider, decode_responses=True)


def get_product(product_id, load_from_db):
    key = f"product:{product_id}"
    cached = r.get(key)
    if cached is not None:
        return json.loads(cached)
    product = load_from_db(product_id)
    r.set(key, json.dumps(product), ex=600)  # expire after ten minutes
    return product


def save_product(product, write_to_db):
    write_to_db(product)
    r.delete(f"product:{product['id']}")  # invalidate after the write succeeds
blocks.title: Python · redis_cache.py (Entra ID, cache-aside, invalidation)

blocks.text:
With RediSearch, Azure Managed Redis works as a low-latency vector database. Store each vector next to the metadata you filter on and return: tenant, category, document ID, timestamp. Index types: FLAT is an exact brute-force index for smaller sets, and HNSW is an approximate graph index for larger sets where latency matters more than an exhaustive search. Distance metrics are L2, COSINE and IP (inner product). Cosine is a common choice for text embeddings, but the right metric depends on the model and on how its vectors are normalized. A KNN query returns the top K most similar vectors, and a range query returns everything within a distance. Hybrid queries combine a metadata filter with the vector search.

Semantic caching reuses an earlier LLM answer when a new prompt means the same as an old one. Embed the prompt, look for a cached entry within a distance threshold that also matches the right partition (tenant, model, prompt version), and return its response. On a miss, call the model and store the prompt, response, embedding, metadata and a TTL. In Python, RedisVL's SemanticCache provides check and store for this. A lower distance threshold is stricter.
blocks.title: Vector indexing and similarity search

blocks.text:
import numpy as np
from redis.commands.search.field import TagField, TextField, VectorField
from redis.commands.search.index_definition import IndexDefinition, IndexType
from redis.commands.search.query import Query

DIM = 1536


def create_index(r):
    fields = (
        TagField("tenant"),
        TextField("body"),
        VectorField("vec", "HNSW",
                    {"TYPE": "FLOAT32", "DIM": DIM, "DISTANCE_METRIC": "COSINE"}),
    )
    r.ft("idx:docs").create_index(
        fields, definition=IndexDefinition(prefix=["doc:"], index_type=IndexType.HASH))


def add(r, doc_id, tenant, body, vec):
    r.hset(f"doc:{doc_id}", mapping={
        "tenant": tenant, "body": body,
        "vec": np.asarray(vec, dtype=np.float32).tobytes()})


def knn(r, tenant, vec, k=4):
    expr = "(@tenant:{%s})=>[KNN %d @vec $v AS dist]" % (tenant, k)
    q = (Query(expr)
         .sort_by("dist").return_fields("body", "dist").dialect(2))
    blob = np.asarray(vec, dtype=np.float32).tobytes()
    return r.ft("idx:docs").search(q, query_params={"v": blob}).docs

blocks.text:
• With Redis 7.4, modules are chosen when you create the cache and can't be added afterwards, and OSS and Enterprise clustering can't be changed in place. Plan module and policy choices before you create it.
• Port 10000 with TLS. Prefer Entra ID, because access keys are disabled on new caches.
• volatile-lru (the default) evicts only keys with a TTL.
• Invalidate on write keeps writes simple but can briefly show old data. Write-through gives read-after-write freshness but costs more per write.
• Repeated, differently worded prompts call for a semantic cache with a distance threshold, not an exact-key cache.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: A catalogue uses cache-aside with invalidate on write, and right after an admin edits a price, a few shoppers briefly see the old price. For the price path only, the team switches to write-through: the update writes the store and the cache in the same operation and returns only when both succeed. Other, rarely read data keeps invalidate on write, because write-through costs more on every write.
blocks.title: Worked scenario

blocks.text: Question: a cache holds tens of millions of tiny keys, each with a TTL, and uses far more memory than the values add up to. Why? Solution: every key carries internal metadata, typically 50 to 100 bytes depending on the key name, and keys with a TTL need extra bookkeeping for expiration. At that scale, shorter key names also save memory.

lessons.title: 3.1 · Azure Service Bus: queues, topics, settlement and dead-lettering
lessons.summary: Queue back-end work reliably: send and receive with the Python SDK, settle messages correctly, fan out with topics and filters, and handle the dead-letter queue.

blocks.text:
Service Bus is a message broker for reliable queuing and durable publish-subscribe. A queue hands each message to one of several competing consumers, in roughly first-in, first-out order. A topic gives a copy of each message to every subscription whose rules match. Consumers read from the subscriptions, never from the topic itself, and each subscription behaves like its own queue.

Receive modes:
• Peek-lock (the default in the Python SDK) is two-stage. The broker locks the message and hands it over, then your code settles it. Settlement options: complete (done), abandon (unlock it now for redelivery), defer (set it aside, to be fetched later by sequence number) or dead-letter (move it to the dead-letter queue with a reason). If the lock expires first, the message becomes available again. The lock lasts 1 minute by default and at most 5 minutes, so renew it for longer work. A crash before complete means redelivery, which makes this at-least-once processing.
• Receive-and-delete marks the message consumed as soon as it's handed over. A crash loses the message, which makes this at-most-once processing.
Settle on the same receiver and connection that received the message. Closing the receiver, or the service's 10-minute idle timeout, releases the lock.
blocks.title: Queues, topics and receive modes

blocks.text:
Every queue and every subscription has a dead-letter queue (DLQ), reached at <queue>/$deadletterqueue or <topic>/Subscriptions/<sub> followed by /$deadletterqueue. Messages land there for several reasons:
• MaxDeliveryCountExceeded: the delivery count passed the maximum, 10 by default. Every abandon, and every lock that runs out before settlement, adds one to the count.
• TTLExpiredException: the message expired while dead-lettering on expiration was enabled.
• A subscription filter threw an error while dead-lettering on filter evaluation exceptions was enabled.
• Your code called dead_letter_message with its own reason and description. Put the exception type in the reason and the details in the description.
Nothing cleans the DLQ automatically. Messages stay until you receive and complete them, so monitor its count, read it by passing sub_queue set to ServiceBusSubQueue.DEAD_LETTER and fix the cause, then resubmit or discard. A message that can't be auto-forwarded goes to the transfer dead-letter queue of the source entity, and forwarding stops after 4 hops (MaxTransferHopCountExceeded).
blocks.title: The dead-letter queue

blocks.text:
• Sessions (session_id on each message) give ordered, FIFO processing of related messages, one session per receiver at a time.
• Duplicate detection drops a resend whose MessageId was already seen within the detection window. Derive the MessageId from the business operation so a retry repeats it.
• Sessions and duplicate detection need the Standard or Premium tier, because Basic offers neither.
• Time to live: if you set nothing, messages and entities default to the maximum possible TTL. A locked message isn't affected by expiry, and the broker may remove expired messages lazily. Schedule delivery with schedule_messages or by setting scheduled_enqueue_time_utc.
• Topic rules: every new subscription starts with a default rule whose filter is the true filter, so it receives everything until you replace that rule. A SQL filter evaluates a SQL-like expression over user properties and system properties (sys. prefix). A correlation filter matches exact property values, and string comparison is case-sensitive. Learn prefers correlation filters where possible, because SQL filters lower throughput. Rules without actions combine with OR into one copy, while each rule with an action produces its own copy.
blocks.title: Sessions, duplicates, expiry and filters

blocks.text:
import json
import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import (AutoLockRenewer, ServiceBusClient, ServiceBusMessage,
                              ServiceBusSubQueue)

FQDN = os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"]  # <namespace>.servicebus.windows.net
credential = DefaultAzureCredential()


def enqueue(invoice_id):
    with ServiceBusClient(FQDN, credential) as client:
        with client.get_queue_sender("invoices") as sender:
            sender.send_messages(ServiceBusMessage(
                json.dumps({"invoice": invoice_id}), message_id=f"inv-{invoice_id}",
                application_properties={"kind": "ocr"}))


def work():
    renewer = AutoLockRenewer(max_lock_renewal_duration=900)
    with ServiceBusClient(FQDN, credential) as client:
        with client.get_queue_receiver("invoices", max_wait_time=30,
                                       auto_lock_renewer=renewer) as receiver:
            for msg in receiver:
                try:
                    job = json.loads(str(msg))
                except ValueError:
                    receiver.dead_letter_message(
                        msg, reason="InvalidJson", error_description="body not JSON")
                    continue
                print("processing", job["invoice"])
                receiver.complete_message(msg)


def inspect_dead_letters():
    with ServiceBusClient(FQDN, credential) as client:
        with client.get_queue_receiver("invoices", max_wait_time=5,
                                       sub_queue=ServiceBusSubQueue.DEAD_LETTER) as dlq:
            for msg in dlq:
                print(msg.dead_letter_reason, msg.delivery_count)
                dlq.complete_message(msg)  # after logging or resubmitting a fixed copy

blocks.text:
• The DLQ has no automatic clean-up. Monitor its count and drain it yourself.
• Each dead-letter reason has its own trigger: delivery count over the maximum, expiry with dead-lettering on expiration enabled, filter errors with that option enabled, or your own call.
• Work that outlasts the lock (1 minute default, 5 maximum) causes redelivery and duplicates. Renew the lock, and make the handler idempotent anyway.
• Ordered processing per customer: sessions. Drop resends: duplicate detection on MessageId. Neither exists in Basic.
• A new subscription receives every message through its default true filter until you replace the rule.
• A range condition such as amount > 5000 needs a SQL filter, because correlation filters match exact values only.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: A billing worker sometimes receives a payment message before the order message it depends on. Rather than abandoning it and burning delivery attempts, the worker calls defer_message and records the payment's sequence number. When the order arrives, it fetches the deferred payment with receive_deferred_messages using that sequence number, processes it and completes it.
blocks.title: Worked scenario

blocks.text: Question: a receiver pulls messages, puts them in an in-memory list and completes them twenty minutes later, and the complete calls start failing. Why? Solution: the lock is tied to the receiver and its connection, and the service closes an idle connection after 10 minutes, which releases the lock (on top of the lock duration itself). Settle promptly on the same receiver, and renew locks if processing is long.

lessons.title: 3.2 · Azure Event Grid: custom events, filters, retries and dead-lettering
lessons.summary: Publish custom events, route them with event type, subject and advanced filters, and understand retries and dead-lettering, naming the delivery model each time.

blocks.text:
Event Grid routes events, which are lightweight notifications that something happened, to subscribers that react to them. Compare Service Bus, which carries high-value messages for transactional work, and Event Hubs, which ingests streams. Sources come in two kinds:
• System topics carry events published by Azure services such as Storage. Only the Azure service can publish to one, so it has no endpoint or keys of its own.
• Custom topics carry your application's events, published to the topic's endpoint. A custom topic accepts the CloudEvents v1.0 schema or the Event Grid schema. CloudEvents is the open, interoperable choice.

Event Grid comes in two models, and facts differ between them:
• Event Grid Basic: system topics, custom topics and domains, with push delivery only. The retry and dead-letter defaults below belong to this model.
• Event Grid Namespaces: namespace topics with pull delivery (consumers receive and then acknowledge, release or reject) as well as push delivery.
In Python, EventGridPublisherClient sends to both models (add namespace_topic= for a namespace), and EventGridConsumerClient handles namespace pull delivery. Authenticate with a topic access key (AzureKeyCredential) or Microsoft Entra ID (DefaultAzureCredential).
blocks.title: Events, topics and the two models

blocks.text:
By default a subscription receives every event type its source emits. Three kinds of filter narrow it:
• Event types: includedEventTypes lists the types to deliver, for example only an app's .Uploaded event.
• Subject: subjectBeginsWith and subjectEndsWith compare a prefix or a suffix of the event's subject (a container path, or a .jpg suffix). Give custom events subjects that are easy to filter on.
• Advanced filters compare a key, which can be event data such as data.sizeMb or, in the CloudEvents schema, attributes such as source or eventtype, against values with an operator: NumberGreaterThan, NumberLessThanOrEquals, StringBeginsWith, StringIn and others. Arrays need advanced filtering on arrays switched on for the subscription. If the key is missing from the event, most operators evaluate as not matched, but NumberNotIn and StringNotIn match, and IsNullOrUndefined evaluates to true.
Limits: 25 advanced filters and 25 filter values across all filters of one subscription, 512 characters per string value, and no keys that contain a dot.
blocks.title: Filtering an event subscription

blocks.text:
Delivery is at least once and not ordered, so make handlers idempotent and order-tolerant. Only 200 to 204 responses count as success. Event Grid waits 30 seconds for a response, then retries with exponential backoff (10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min, 10 min, 30 min, 1 h, 3 h, 6 h, then every 12 hours up to 24 hours) with some randomization.

Each subscription's retry policy has two limits, and whichever runs out first ends delivery:
• maximum delivery attempts, 1 to 30, default 30
• event time to live, 1 to 1,440 minutes, default 1,440 (24 hours)
TTL is checked only at the next scheduled attempt.

Some errors are never retried: 400 and 413, plus 403 for Azure resource endpoints and 401 and 403 for webhooks. Dead-lettering is off by default. Without it, those events and events that exhaust their retries are dropped. Turn it on by giving the subscription a Blob Storage container as its dead-letter location. A 400 or 413 response then dead-letters the event immediately. Writes happen about five minutes after the last attempt, and if the storage location stays unavailable for four hours the event is dropped.
blocks.title: Delivery, retries and dead-lettering (Event Grid Basic push delivery)

blocks.text: A webhook endpoint must prove that it wants events before it receives any. For Event Grid schema subscriptions, Event Grid sends a SubscriptionValidationEvent (Microsoft.EventGrid event type). The endpoint either echoes the validationCode in its response or, later, calls the validationUrl, which stays valid for 10 minutes. CloudEvents v1.0 delivery uses its own abuse protection: an HTTP OPTIONS request with a WebHook-Request-Origin header that the endpoint must answer. Azure Functions with the Event Grid trigger, Logic Apps and Azure Automation handle this for you.
blocks.title: Webhook validation

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.core.credentials import AzureKeyCredential
from azure.core.messaging import CloudEvent
from azure.eventgrid import EventGridConsumerClient, EventGridPublisherClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

# Event Grid Basic custom topic (CloudEvents schema), access key auth
publisher = EventGridPublisherClient(os.environ["EG_TOPIC_ENDPOINT"],
                                     AzureKeyCredential(os.environ["EG_TOPIC_KEY"]))

blocks.text: A thumbnail function behind an Event Grid Basic subscription returned 503 for twenty minutes during a deployment. lessons.title: 3.3 · Azure Functions: triggers, bindings, configuration and deployment
lessons.summary: Build serverless APIs with the Python v2 programming model, wire triggers and bindings, then choose a hosting plan, configure settings and deploy.

blocks.text:
A function has exactly one trigger, which starts it, and any number of input and output bindings, which read and write data declaratively. The Python v2 programming model is the one recommended for new apps. You declare everything with decorators on a func.FunctionApp() object in function_app.py, with no function.json files. The v1 model, with a function.json file and __init__.py per function, is for legacy apps. Larger apps put functions in blueprints (bp = func.Blueprint()) and register them with app.register_functions(bp).

Common decorators:
• @app.route(route=..., methods=[...], auth_level=...) for HTTP.
• @app.timer_trigger with a schedule for timers. NCRONTAB has six fields, {second} {minute} {hour} {day} {month} {day-of-week}, so 0 */5 * * * * runs every five minutes.
• @app.service_bus_queue_trigger and @app.cosmos_db_trigger and @app.event_grid_trigger and others for events and messages.
• Output bindings such as @app.service_bus_queue_output. The function writes through a func.Out[...] parameter by calling .set(value).
Inside an HTTP function, read route parameters from req.route_params instead of adding them as arguments. An HTTP function that sets no output returns 204 No Content.

Authorization levels: with any level other than anonymous, callers must send an access key in the x-functions-key header or the code query string. The function level accepts a function key or a host key, and the admin level needs the master key. Keys are shared secrets, not user sign-in. For real authentication, put App Service Authentication or API Management in front.

Connections: a binding's connection value names an app setting or a setting prefix. For identity-based connections you set the prefix plus __fullyQualifiedNamespace (Service Bus, Event Hubs) or the prefix plus __accountEndpoint (Cosmos DB), and give the app's managed identity a data-plane role, so no secret is stored.

blocks.text:
• Flex Consumption is GA, runs on Linux only and is the plan Learn recommends for new serverless apps. It scales to zero and out to 1,000 instances, with each function scaling independently. Instance memory is 512, 2,048 (the default choice for most apps) or 4,096 MB. It offers always-ready instances to cut cold starts and virtual network integration, but no deployment slots. Its container image support and its zero-downtime rolling updates are both preview.
• Premium (Elastic Premium) and Dedicated (App Service plan) suit apps that need prewarmed or reserved capacity, deployment slots or containers.
• Container Apps can host containerized function apps.
• Consumption is now a legacy plan. Hosting on Linux Consumption retires on 30 September 2028 and gets no new features or language versions, and apps still on the v3 runtime there stop after 30 September 2026. For new apps, choose Flex Consumption.
The Python runtime runs only on Linux, on every plan. Default function timeouts are 30 minutes on Flex Consumption, Premium, Dedicated and Container Apps, and 5 minutes (maximum 10) on Consumption. Whatever the timeout, an HTTP-triggered function must respond within 230 seconds, or the load balancer returns 502 while the function keeps running. For longer work, follow an async pattern: accept the request, queue the job and return a status location.

blocks.text:
• host.json carries runtime settings for the whole app, functionTimeout for example, and deploys with your code.
• App settings reach your code as environment variables. They hold connections (AzureWebJobsStorage, identity-based prefixes) and app configuration.
• local.settings.json is for local runs only and is never published. Add the same values as app settings in Azure. Because it can hold secrets, keep it out of source control.
• requirements.txt lists Python packages, which a remote build installs during deployment.
Deployment: func azure functionapp publish (Core Tools) packages and deploys the project. Flex Consumption has a deployment method of its own: the zip goes into a blob deployment container, and the app reads it from there at startup. The az functionapp deployment source config-zip command works there too. On Flex Consumption you can't use classic ZIP deployment, external package URLs (WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE), source control, local Git or FTPS. The other plans support them.
