lessons.title: 4.1 · Key Vault secrets and App Configuration
lessons.summary: Retrieve and rotate secrets with Key Vault and the right RBAC roles, and centralize settings, labels, feature flags and dynamic refresh with App Configuration.

blocks.text:
The azure-keyvault-secrets package provides SecretClient, which you create with the vault URL and a DefaultAzureCredential. The same code then uses your developer sign-in locally and the managed identity in Azure. set_secret creates a secret, or a new version of an existing one. get_secret(name) returns the latest version, and get_secret(name, version) returns a specific one. update_secret_properties changes metadata such as content_type, enabled, expires_on and tags without creating a new version. list_properties_of_secrets lists metadata only, never values. begin_delete_secret starts a delete that you can recover from.

Access: Azure RBAC is the recommended permission model. Learn recommends a vault per application per environment, with roles assigned at vault scope rather than on individual secrets.
• Key Vault Secrets User reads secret contents.
• Key Vault Secrets Officer can do anything with secrets except manage permissions.
• Key Vault Reader reads metadata only and can't see values.
Watch who holds Contributor on the vault, because with the access policy model a control-plane Contributor can grant themselves data access.
blocks.title: Key Vault secrets from Python

blocks.text:
Soft delete is on by default for new vaults and can't be turned off once enabled. Deleted vaults and objects stay recoverable for 7 to 90 days (90 by default). You set that period only at vault creation and can't change it later. A soft-deleted vault's name can't be reused until the period ends. Purge protection is optional and off by default, needs soft delete, and stops anyone purging a deleted vault or object before the retention period passes.

Key Vault throttles heavy callers (429). Honour exponential back-off, cache secrets in memory and re-read only when the cached copy stops working (after a rotation, for example), and split traffic across vaults per app and region. Where the target service supports Microsoft Entra ID, skip the secret entirely and use a managed identity.

Rotation is event-driven. Key Vault publishes a SecretNearExpiry event (Microsoft.KeyVault namespace) to Event Grid 30 days before the current version's expiry date, alongside SecretExpired and SecretNewVersionCreated. A typical rotator is an Event Grid-triggered function that creates a new credential, writes it as a new secret version and updates the target service. For services with two keys, such as storage accounts, store the keys as alternating versions and regenerate the key that isn't current, so one valid key always exists.
blocks.title: Protection, throttling and rotation

blocks.text:
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.keyvault.secrets import SecretClient

client = SecretClient(vault_url=os.environ["KEY_VAULT_URL"],
                      credential=DefaultAzureCredential())

# A new version with an expiry date, so SecretNearExpiry fires 30 days before it
client.set_secret("partner-token", os.environ["NEW_PARTNER_TOKEN"],
                  content_type="text/plain",
                  expires_on=datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(days=60))

_cache = {}


def secret(name, max_age=600.0):
    value, fetched_at = _cache.get(name, (None, 0.0))
    if value is None or time.monotonic() - fetched_at > max_age:
        value = client.get_secret(name).value  # latest version
        _cache[name] = (value, time.monotonic())
    return value


for props in client.list_properties_of_secrets():  # metadata only
    print(props.name, props.enabled, props.expires_on)
blocks.title: Python · secrets.py (azure-keyvault-secrets)

blocks.text:
App Configuration stores non-secret settings and feature flags centrally, so many apps and environments share one source without redeploying.
• Keys are case-sensitive strings, usually hierarchical (Checkout:Payments:Timeout). A key-value can be at most 10 KB.
• Labels create variants of the same key, typically one per environment. Unlabelled key-values have no label (the selector writes this as "\0").
• The Python provider is azure-appconfiguration-provider. Its load() loads unlabelled key-values by default. With selects=[SettingSelector(...)] you choose keys and labels, and when several selectors return the same key, the last selector wins. trim_prefixes strips a prefix from the key names, and a selector can also load a snapshot.
• Dynamic refresh: refresh_on with WatchKey("Sentinel") watches a sentinel key, refresh_interval defaults to 30 seconds, and your code calls config.refresh(). Update the sentinel last, after all related keys, so apps reload a consistent set.
• Key Vault references keep secrets in Key Vault. The provider resolves them with keyvault_credential, so the app's identity must hold two roles: App Configuration Data Reader on the store and Key Vault Secrets User on the vault.
• Feature flags load with feature_flag_enabled=True. The featuremanagement package's FeatureManager then evaluates them, with filters such as targeting, time window and percentage. Metric scorecards for flags are preview.
• Data-plane roles: App Configuration Data Reader (read) and App Configuration Data Owner (read, write, delete). Neither grants access to manage the store resource itself.
blocks.title: Azure App Configuration

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.appconfiguration.provider import SettingSelector, WatchKey, load
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
config = load(
    endpoint=os.environ["APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT"],
    credential=credential,
    selects=[SettingSelector(key_filter="Checkout:*", label_filter="\0"),
             SettingSelector(key_filter="Checkout:*", label_filter="prod")],
    trim_prefixes=["Checkout:"],
    keyvault_credential=credential,    # resolves Key Vault references
    refresh_on=[WatchKey("Checkout:Sentinel")],
    refresh_interval=60,
)


def payment_timeout():
    config.refresh()  # checks the sentinel only when the interval has passed
    return int(config["Payments:TimeoutSeconds"])
blocks.title: Python · settings.py (azure-appconfiguration-provider)

blocks.text:
• Reading secret values needs Key Vault Secrets User. Key Vault Reader can't see values, and Secrets Officer is for management.
• Rotation trigger: the Key Vault SecretNearExpiry event, 30 days before expiry, through Event Grid.
• The soft-delete retention period is fixed at vault creation. Purge protection is off until you enable it.
• Secrets stay in Key Vault and App Configuration holds references. The app's identity needs access to both.
• Settings don't change until a refresh: watch a sentinel, update it last and call refresh().
• Per-environment values: labels, not a separate key name for each environment. The last matching selector wins.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Three services keep their checkout timeouts and payment endpoint in local environment files, so every change means three redeployments. Move the values to App Configuration as Checkout:* keys with dev and prod labels. Put the payment token in Key Vault and reference it from App Configuration. Give each service's managed identity App Configuration Data Reader and Key Vault Secrets User, and load with a sentinel watch. A change is now two writes, the value and then the sentinel, and every service picks it up within its refresh interval.
blocks.title: Worked scenario

blocks.text: Question: Learn recommends assigning Key Vault roles at vault scope. When does it accept role assignments on individual secrets? Solution: in exceptions, such as a secret that a single user must read (an SSH private key used through Azure Bastion) or a secret that several applications share. Otherwise use one vault per application per environment, with roles at vault scope.

lessons.title: 4.2 · OpenTelemetry tracing and KQL
lessons.summary: Instrument Python services with an OpenTelemetry distro for Azure Monitor, follow one operation across services, and write KQL against the Application Insights tables.

blocks.text:
A trace is a tree of spans that share one operation ID. Each span is a unit of work, such as a request, a database call or a model call, with a start time, a duration, attributes and a status. In Application Insights, operation_Id (OperationId in the workspace tables) groups the telemetry of one end-to-end operation, and W3C Trace Context carries the trace across service boundaries.

Two Python packages send OpenTelemetry data to Application Insights. Don't initialize both in one app.
• The Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro, package microsoft-opentelemetry. Learn's Python pages now lead with it: from microsoft.opentelemetry import use_microsoft_opentelemetry, then call use_microsoft_opentelemetry with enable_azure_monitor=True, which reads the connection string from the Application Insights connection string environment variable (named in the code below). Apps already on the older distro need no action.
• The Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro, package azure-monitor-opentelemetry, documented in the Python API reference. You call configure_azure_monitor() once at startup. It accepts connection_string= or reads the same environment variable, collects traces, metrics and logs (logger_name selects your application logger), and enables bundled instrumentations for Django, FastAPI, Flask, httpx, psycopg2, requests, urllib and urllib3. An environment variable (named in the code below) switches some of them off.
The code below uses the second package, because the API reference documents it in full.
blocks.title: Two Python distros, named by package

blocks.text:
• Cloud role name, the node name on the Application Map, comes from the resource attributes service.namespace and service.name, falling back to service.name alone. Cloud role instance comes from service.instance.id. Set them with OTEL_SERVICE_NAME and OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES. If every service shows up as the same node, this is what to fix.
• Sampling: both distros default to rate-limited sampling of five traces per second (the Microsoft distro per Learn's sampling page, azure-monitor-opentelemetry per its README), so the sample below starts at that rate too. The two strategies are fixed-rate (a ratio between 0 and 1) and rate-limited (traces per second). With azure-monitor-opentelemetry, set OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER to microsoft.fixed_percentage or microsoft.rate_limited, with OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG, or pass traces_per_second.
• Custom telemetry: get a tracer with trace.get_tracer(__name__) and open spans with tracer.start_as_current_span. Exceptions raised inside a span are recorded automatically, or call span.record_exception() yourself. A SpanProcessor's on_start can add attributes (span.set_attribute) to every span. When a job runs outside any instrumented request (a scheduled batch, say), create its span with kind=SpanKind.SERVER so Application Insights records it as a request.
• Live Metrics is on by default and carries a preview-terms notice in its Learn section.
blocks.title: Configuration that matters

blocks.text:
import logging

from azure.monitor.opentelemetry import configure_azure_monitor
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.trace import SpanKind

# Reads APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING; call once, at startup.
# OTEL_PYTHON_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS=psycopg2 would skip one instrumentation.
configure_azure_monitor(logger_name="orders")

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)
log = logging.getLogger("orders")


def nightly_settlement(batch):
    # A background job: SERVER kind makes it show up as a request.
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("settle-batch", kind=SpanKind.SERVER) as span:
        span.set_attribute("app.batch_size", len(batch))
        for order in batch:
            with tracer.start_as_current_span("settle-order"):
                log.info("settled %s", order)  # log records join the active span
blocks.title: Python · telemetry.py (azure-monitor-opentelemetry)

blocks.text:
A KQL query is a pipeline: a table, then operators joined by |.
• Filter early on time: where TimeGenerated > ago(1h), then the other conditions.
• Shape: project picks and renames columns, extend adds computed ones, and take, top N by and order by trim and sort. Finish exploratory queries with limit or count so they stay small.
• Aggregate: summarize count(), countif(), avg() or percentile(DurationMs, 95) by a column or by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m). percentiles() computes several at once, and render timechart (or barchart, columnchart and others) draws the result.
• Combine: join kind=inner or kind=leftouter on a key such as OperationId. The default join flavour is innerunique, which removes duplicate keys from the left side first.
• Strings: == is case-sensitive and =~ isn't. has matches whole terms through the term index (terms of three characters or more), while contains matches any substring and is slower. Learn's best practices prefer has.
Workspace-based Application Insights data lives in App* tables. The pages saved for this pack show AppRequests (Name, DurationMs, Success, ResultCode, OperationId, AppRoleName), AppDependencies (Target, DependencyType, DurationMs, Success) and AppExceptions (ExceptionType, OuterMessage, ProblemId).
From Python, azure-monitor-query's LogsQueryClient runs KQL with query_workspace(workspace_id, query, timespan=...). A result can come back partial (LogsQueryStatus.PARTIAL, with partial_error and partial_data). Since version 2.0, metrics queries have moved to the separate azure-monitor-querymetrics package.
blocks.title: KQL essentials

blocks.text:
// p95 latency and failure count per operation in 15-minute buckets
AppRequests
| where TimeGenerated > ago(12h) and AppRoleName == "orders-api"
| summarize p95 = percentile(DurationMs, 95), failed = countif(Success == false),
    total = count() by Name, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| extend failedPct = round(100.0 * failed / total, 1)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// The slowest dependency calls behind failed requests
AppRequests
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h) and Success == false
| project OperationId, RequestName = Name
| join kind=inner (AppDependencies | where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)) on OperationId
| top 10 by DurationMs desc
| project TimeGenerated, RequestName, Target, DependencyType, DurationMs
blocks.title: KQL · slow and failing operations, then their dependencies

import os
from datetime import timedelta

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.monitor.query import LogsQueryClient, LogsQueryStatus

client = LogsQueryClient(DefaultAzureCredential())
query = "AppExceptions | summarize hits = count() by ExceptionType | top 5 by hits"
result = client.query_workspace(os.environ["LOG_WORKSPACE_ID"], query,
                                timespan=timedelta(days=1))
if result.status == LogsQueryStatus.SUCCESS:
    tables = result.tables
else:
    print("partial result:", result.partial_error)
    tables = result.partial_data
for table in tables:
    for row in table.rows:
        print(list(row))

• Name the package: microsoft-opentelemetry uses use_microsoft_opentelemetry, and azure-monitor-opentelemetry uses configure_azure_monitor. Never initialize both.
• Cloud role name = service.namespace plus service.name (or service.name alone); cloud role instance = service.instance.id.

The library can still be instrumented by hand later if a specific query needs tracing.

questions.prompt: Container apps in West Europe and East US pull a large image from a Standard registry in West Europe, and pulls in East US are slow. You need one registry name with network-close pulls in both regions. What should you do?

options.text: Keep Standard and rely on its default zone redundancy in West Europe
Upgrade the registry to Premium and add an East US geo-replica
Reference the image by digest instead of by tag in the East US apps
Create a second Standard registry in East US and push each build to both

questions.explanation: Geo-replication is a Premium feature that keeps one registry name while serving pulls from a replica in each chosen region, so East US pulls no longer travel to West Europe. A second registry means a second name and a second push for every build, and zone redundancy only spreads data across zones inside one region. Pulling by digest changes which image is pulled, not where it's served from.

questions.prompt: A team wants every production rollback to pull exactly the build that was tested. Which TWO image references should its deployments use? Select TWO.

A major-version tag such as 1
A minor-version tag such as 1.4 that receives patches
The manifest digest (sha256) of the build
The latest tag, re-pushed after each build

questions.explanation: A unique tag is never reused and a digest identifies one exact manifest, so both keep pointing at the tested image after later pushes; Learn recommends unique tags for deployments. Stable tags such as latest, 1 or 1.4 are moved to newer images as patches ship, so a rollback through them can pull an image that was never tested.

--read-enabled false
--delete-enabled false

questions.explanation: Setting write-enabled to false locks a tag against both overwrite and deletion, whereas delete-enabled false on its own still lets a push replace the tag. On a repository, delete-enabled false with write-enabled true stops deletion of the repository while pushes keep working; write-enabled false would lock every image in it. Only read-enabled false blocks pulls, because the write and delete flags leave reads allowed.

questions.prompt: A nightly build re-pushes docs-api:3 with OS patches, and registry storage keeps growing although the number of tags stays flat. What should you do?

Switch the nightly build to unique build-ID tags instead of docs-api:3
Move the registry to a tier that includes more storage in its daily rate
Delete the untagged manifests left behind, by manifest digest

questions.explanation: When a stable tag such as 3 moves to a new build, the previous manifest loses its tag but stays in the registry with its unique layers, so storage climbs while the tag list looks unchanged; deleting those manifests by digest removes them and their unique layer data. acr purge --untagged in a scheduled task and the Premium retention policy can automate this, but both are preview, and the policy covers only manifests untagged after it takes effect. Locking the tag would break the nightly patch builds, and unique tags or a larger tier leave the old manifests in place.

questions.prompt: For each statement about Azure Container Registry tiers, select Yes or No.

questions.prompt: A pipeline agent has no Docker engine, but the pipeline must build the Dockerfile in the repository and push the result to the contosoai registry. Which command should the pipeline run?

Signing in and then running docker build and docker push still needs an engine on the agent, az acr import only copies an image that already exists, and az acr task logs shows the output of earlier runs.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order so that docs-api is rebuilt automatically whenever its Python base image is patched.

Run the task once with az acr task run so that it records the base image dependency
Import the patched version of the base image into contosoai
Import the Python base image into contosoai and create a task that builds FROM the imported image

questions.explanation: Keeping a copy of the base image in your own registry means an update triggers the task at once instead of after a 10 to 60 minute check of the public repository. The task, whose base image trigger is on by default, has to run once before ACR Tasks knows the dependency; after that, updating the image behind the stable tag starts a rebuild, and runs started by a trigger keep their logs for az acr task logs.

questions.prompt: Match each build requirement to the ACR Tasks feature that meets it.

options.text: Timer trigger
Pull request trigger
Source code commit trigger
Quick task (az acr build)
Base image update trigger

Rebuild when the FROM image receives OS patches
Run an image maintenance step every night
Build once from a laptop that has no Docker engine

questions.explanation: Commit triggers, on by default for a Git context, react to pushes; base image triggers react to updates of the image named in FROM; timer triggers run a task on a schedule; and az acr build is the on-demand quick task. A pull request trigger is off by default and fires when a pull request is opened or updated, so it fits none of these requirements.

questions.prompt: An ACR task builds FROM python:3.12.7-slim. The maintainers then publish python:3.12.8-slim, yet the task never runs. Why?

options.text: Base image tracking works for images in Azure registries, not Docker Hub

A new version tag leaves 3.12.7-slim untouched; build FROM a stable tag like 3.12-slim
Base image triggers are off by default and must be enabled on each task

questions.explanation: A base image trigger fires when the image behind the referenced tag is updated, and publishing a new version tag leaves 3.12.7-slim exactly as it was. Building from a stable tag such as 3.12-slim, which the maintainers move to each patch, lets the trigger fire. Base image triggers are enabled by default, and public Docker Hub and Microsoft Container Registry images are checked every 10 to 60 minutes.

questions.prompt: A Linux custom container on App Service runs gunicorn on port 8000, and the site fails to start because the platform sends requests to port 80. What should you configure?

The WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE app setting set to true
The WEBSITES_PORT app setting with the value 8000
The CONTAINER_AVAILABILITY_CHECK_MODE app setting set to Repair

questions.explanation: App Service assumes a custom container listens on port 80 and forwards traffic to the port named in WEBSITES_PORT when it listens elsewhere; only one HTTP port can be exposed. Docker Compose ignores ports other than 80 and 8080 and is being retired in favour of sidecars, the storage setting only controls whether /home persists, and the availability check mode applies to Windows containers.

within 24 hours

Without a pinned version, App Service caches resolved values and fetches them again every 24 hours, or at once when a configuration change restarts the app; 30 minutes is the Container Apps refresh window.

questions.prompt: Which TWO actions let App Service pull its image from Azure Container Registry without storing any registry credentials? Select TWO.

Enable the registry admin user and save its password as an app setting

The admin user means storing a password, a Key Vault role grants nothing on the registry, and the storage setting only controls /home persistence.

questions.prompt: Staging and production slots must each keep their own Key Vault reference, pointing at kv-staging and kv-prod, after every swap. What should you do?

options.text: Give the production slot's identity access to the staging vault
Mark each Key Vault reference setting as a deployment slot setting
Pin each reference to a specific secret version in its URI
Put both references in one setting separated by a semicolon

questions.explanation: Slot settings stay with their slot during a swap, so each environment keeps the reference to its own vault; Learn suggests this for most Key Vault references because each environment should have a separate vault. Two references in one setting don't form a valid reference, pinning a version controls rotation rather than swap behaviour, and cross-vault access mixes the environments.

questions.prompt: After a deployment, an App Service container reads the literal text @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...) from its OPENAI_KEY setting instead of the key. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Linux custom containers receive changed app settings only after a manual restart of the app
The secret was rotated recently, and its new version reaches the app within 24 hours
App settings that hold references must be resolved in code with the Key Vault SDK
The reference wasn't resolved, for example because the identity can't read the secret

questions.explanation: When App Service can't resolve a Key Vault reference, it passes the reference string itself to the app, most often because the identity lacks Key Vault Secrets User or a Get permission, the secret no longer exists, or the syntax is wrong; the setting's edit dialog and the Key Vault Application Settings Diagnostics detector show the reason. References need no code changes, a pending rotation still delivers the previous value, and changing an app setting restarts the app by itself, with no manual step.

questions.prompt: Which change to a container app creates a new revision?

options.text: Changing traffic weights between revisions
Adding a secret to the app
Updating the image tag in the app template
Switching ingress from external to internal

questions.explanation: Revision-scope settings live under properties.template, such as the container image, its environment variables and scale rules, and changing them creates a new revision. Secrets, traffic weights and ingress settings live under properties.configuration, so they apply to every revision without creating one.

a label assigned to docs-api--v2

questions.prompt: You run az containerapp create with --secrets that use keyvaultref and set identityref to the system-assigned identity, and creation fails. What should you change?

Move the keyvaultref value from --secrets into --env-vars
Wait for the system-assigned identity's role assignment to propagate, then retry
Use a user-assigned identity that already has access to the vault

questions.explanation: During az containerapp create the app's system-assigned identity doesn't exist yet, so a Key Vault reference can only resolve through a user-assigned identity that was given Key Vault Secrets User beforehand. Waiting can't help an identity that is created only with the app, Log Analytics plays no part in secrets, and environment variables point at secrets with secretref instead of holding keyvaultref values.

questions.prompt: You changed the value of the embeddings-key secret stored directly in a container app, but the running revision still uses the old value. What should you do?

options.text: Switch the app from single to multiple revision mode
Wait up to 30 minutes for the platform to refresh the value
Run az containerapp secret set again with the same value
Restart the active revision or deploy a new revision

questions.explanation: Secrets are application-scoped: changing one creates no revision and doesn't reach running replicas, so you restart the revision or deploy a new one to load the value. The automatic refresh within 30 minutes applies to Key Vault references without a version, not to values stored in the app, and neither the revision mode nor sending the same value again reloads it.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements describe a Workload profiles environment in Container Apps? Select TWO.

options.text: It can't scale any app to zero replicas
It's the legacy type kept for older environments
It's the default type for new environments
It supports the Consumption plan and nothing else
It supports both the Consumption and Dedicated plans

questions.explanation: Workload profiles is the default environment type, and it can run apps on the Consumption plan, with scale to zero, as well as on Dedicated workload profiles with reserved hardware. The Consumption only type is the legacy one, and it is the type that supports only the Consumption plan.

questions.prompt: Contoso's test and production container apps must never share compute and must write logs to different workspaces. What should you do?

options.text: Create a separate Container Apps environment for each stage
Use one container app in multiple revision mode with labels test and prod
Keep one environment and give each app its own dedicated workload profile
Keep one environment and set the test app's ingress to internal

questions.explanation: Learn advises separate environments when apps must never share compute or must be isolated by stage, and logging is configured per environment, so two environments give two workspaces. A dedicated workload profile in a shared environment still sends every app's logs to the environment's one destination, labels only route traffic between revisions of one app, and internal ingress changes reachability, not isolation.

questions.prompt: docs-worker uses an azure-servicebus scale rule with messageCount 5, minReplicas 0 and maxReplicas 20, and 47 messages are waiting. What desiredReplicas value does the scaling algorithm compute? Answer in replicas. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: Container Apps computes desiredReplicas as the ceiling of the current metric divided by the target, so ceil(47 / 5) gives 10, which is below maxReplicas 20. The app then grows toward that number in steps of 1, 4, 8 and so on, and it never goes past the configured maximum.

questions.prompt: A queue worker in Container Apps has ingress disabled, a minimum of zero replicas and no scale rules, and it never processes a message. What fixes it?

options.text: Raise the scale limit maxReplicas from 10 to 30 on the worker
Enable external ingress so that KEDA can poll the queue
Add an azure-servicebus scale rule, or set minReplicas to 1
Switch the worker to multiple revision mode

questions.explanation: With ingress disabled and no custom rule, only the default HTTP rule applies, and no HTTP traffic can arrive, so the app stays at zero replicas with no way to start. An azure-servicebus rule lets KEDA start replicas from the queue length, or minReplicas 1 keeps one running. KEDA polls the event source itself, so ingress isn't needed, and a higher maximum or another revision mode doesn't start a replica.

questions.prompt: Which TWO can a Container Apps scale rule use to authenticate to Azure Service Bus? Select TWO.

options.text: An Event Grid subscription key for the namespace
The KEDA operator's cluster-admin service account
The environment's Log Analytics shared key
A managed identity that has access to the namespace
An app secret mapped to the trigger's connection parameter

questions.explanation: Scale rules accept a Container Apps secret mapped to the scaler's trigger parameter (--scale-rule-auth on the CLI) and, for Azure Queue Storage, Service Bus and Event Hubs, a managed identity (--scale-rule-identity, set with the CLI or a template rather than the portal), which Learn prefers because no secret is stored. Container Apps runs KEDA for you, so there's no operator account to use, and Log Analytics or Event Grid keys don't grant access to a queue.

questions.prompt: After the last queue message is processed, a scale-to-zero worker keeps one replica for about five minutes before it stops. Which setting causes this delay?

options.text: The cool down period
The polling interval
The HTTP concurrency target
The scale down stabilization window

questions.explanation: The cool down period, 300 seconds by default, is how long KEDA waits after the last event before it takes a revision from its final replica to zero, and it has no effect while other replicas are removed. The scale down stabilization window delays scale-in decisions while load falls, the polling interval (30 seconds) sets how often the queue is checked, and the HTTP concurrency target drives HTTP rules only.

questions.prompt: New catalog-api pods on AKS show ImagePullBackOff, and the image and tag exist in acrcatalog.azurecr.io. What should you do?

Change the catalog-api Service type from ClusterIP to LoadBalancer
Add a liveness probe to the deployment manifest
Raise the memory limit of the catalog-api container

Memory limits, probes and the Service type act only once a container has been pulled and started, so they can't fix a pull failure.

questions.prompt: Match each Kubernetes object or setting to its purpose.

options.text: Keeps a minimum number of pods up during voluntary disruptions
Gives a set of pods one stable IP address and DNS name
Decides whether a pod receives traffic from a Service
Runs a set number of identical pods and rolls out updates
Restarts a container that stops responding

readinessProbe

Restarting an unresponsive container is the liveness probe's job.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to deploy the catalog-api manifest to AKS from the command line and test it from the internet.

Remove the app with kubectl delete -f catalog-api.yaml

A LoadBalancer Service shows EXTERNAL-IP as pending until Azure assigns a public address, which you then open in a browser, and kubectl delete with the same file removes what apply created.

questions.prompt: Which Kubernetes Service type gives the catalog-api pods a public IP address that Azure manages for internet clients?

options.text: LoadBalancer
ExternalName
NodePort
ClusterIP

questions.explanation: A LoadBalancer Service makes AKS create an Azure load balancer resource with an external IP address and rules that forward to the pods. ClusterIP, the default, gives an address reachable only inside the cluster, NodePort maps a port on each node's own address, and ExternalName creates a DNS entry.

questions.prompt: A Deployment runs 4 replicas with a RollingUpdate strategy and maxUnavailable set to 1. How many pods, at minimum, stay available during an update? Answer in pods. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: maxUnavailable caps how many of the desired pods may be unavailable at once during a rolling update, so with 4 replicas and a value of 1, at least 3 pods keep serving. maxSurge works the other way: it allows extra pods above the desired count while new ones start.

questions.prompt: A Python model server takes about two minutes to load its model, and the kubelet keeps restarting it because the liveness probe fails during loading. What should you add?

options.text: A second replica so that one pod can serve traffic
A startup probe, so the other probes wait until the app has started
A readiness probe that uses the same endpoint as the liveness probe
A PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable set to 1

questions.explanation: When a startup probe is configured, the kubelet runs the readiness and liveness probes only after it succeeds, so a slow model load is no longer mistaken for a hung container. A readiness probe only takes a pod out of load balancing and doesn't stop the liveness probe from restarting it, while a disruption budget or an extra replica protects availability, not the startup of each pod.

questions.prompt: catalog-api pods are in CrashLoopBackOff, and you need the output the container wrote just before it crashed. Which command shows it?

options.text: kubectl get events --watch
kubectl describe deployment catalog-api
kubectl top pod <pod>
kubectl logs <pod> --previous

questions.explanation: kubectl logs with --previous returns the log of the last terminated instance of the container, which holds its exit messages, while plain kubectl logs shows the attempt that is running now. Events and describe output show scheduling and status changes, and top shows resource use, not what the application printed.

Pods that aren't ready don't become endpoints, so an empty endpoints list explains a silent Service. Container Apps system logs carry platform events such as image pulls and probe failures, console logs carry your process output, and ACR task logs cover image builds only.

questions.prompt: A new docs-api revision never becomes ready: system logs show readiness probe failures on port 80, and the new image runs gunicorn on port 8000. What should you change?

questions.prompt: From a debug pod in the frontend namespace, curl to the ClusterIP and port of the orders service in the backend namespace succeeds, but a DNS lookup of orders.backend.svc.cluster.local fails. Which TWO should you check next? Select TWO.

questions.prompt: A Python service knows an item's id and partition key value, and by_id holds a parameterized SELECT on c.id. Which call returns that item for the fewest RUs?

Cosmos DB Operator manages accounts without data access, and a client built with DefaultAzureCredential sends Entra tokens, so it needs no account key.

questions.prompt: A query sorts with ORDER BY c.docType ASC, c.updatedAt DESC and fails because no matching index exists. What should you add to the indexing policy?

A composite index of updatedAt descending, then docType ascending
Included range paths /docType/? and /updatedAt/?
A composite index of docType ascending, then updatedAt descending

Swapping the paths breaks the sequence, docType ascending with updatedAt ascending matches neither the query's directions nor their full reversal, and ordinary range paths support single-property sorts only.

questions.prompt: Users must see their own profile edits at once, other users may see them a little later, and reads should cost as few RUs as possible. Which default consistency level fits?

options.text: Session
Strong
Eventual
Bounded staleness

questions.explanation: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes inside a client session while reading from a single replica, so its reads cost the same as the weaker levels. Strong and bounded staleness read from two replicas and charge about twice the RUs per read, and eventual consistency can hand even the writer a stale copy.

questions.prompt: Chunk items of about 2 KB hold a 1,024-dimension vector in embedding and long text in content, queries filter on tenantId and docType, and writes cost too many RUs. Which TWO changes cut write RUs and keep those filters efficient? Select TWO.

options.text: Change the account default consistency to Eventual

Add a composite index on /content and /embedding
Add /embedding/* to the excluded paths
Add /tenantId/? to the excluded paths

questions.explanation: Every indexed path adds to the RU charge of each write, and neither the vector array nor the long text is used in a range filter, so excluding /embedding/* and /content/? lowers write cost while the root include keeps tenantId and docType indexed; vector search relies on its own vector index. Disabling indexing or excluding /tenantId/? would turn the filters into scans, a composite index adds index work, and write RU cost is the same at every consistency level.

questions.prompt: Query metrics for SELECT VALUE c.title FROM c WHERE UPPER(c.title) = @t show 60,000 retrieved documents, 7 output documents and 0% index utilization. What should you change?

options.text: Add a composite index on title ascending and on id ascending
Request bigger pages so that the query makes fewer round trips
Store an uppercase copy of title at write time and filter on it
Pass populate_index_metrics=True so the query picks its index

questions.explanation: The index can't evaluate UPPER, so the engine loads every document to test the filter, which is what the retrieved count and the zero index utilization show. Saving the uppercase value when the item is written, or indexing it as a computed property, lets a plain equality filter use the index. No composite index can serve the function either, the index-metrics flag only reports index use, and larger pages don't reduce the documents the query must load.

questions.prompt: A container will hold about 3 million 3,072-dimension embeddings, and searches must keep latency and RU cost low across the whole set. Which vector index type should you choose?

flat

range

questions.explanation: diskANN is the approximate index built for large search scopes, generally the best performer beyond about 50,000 vectors, with the lowest latency and RU cost, and it accepts up to 4,096 dimensions. flat stops at 505 dimensions, quantizedFlat is a brute-force scan over compressed vectors that suits scopes of 50,000 or fewer, and range belongs to the standard index, not the vector index types.

questions.explanation: float16 stores each element in half the space of float32 with some loss of accuracy, and euclidean measures straight-line distance, where smaller values mean closer vectors. flat is a brute-force search with full recall for vectors of up to 505 dimensions, and quantizedFlat scans compressed vectors, which suits searches that filters have narrowed to a small set. Dot product is a similarity in which larger values mean more similar, so it matches none of the rows.

questions.prompt: A new container holds 600 chunk vectors under a diskANN index, and vector queries cost far more RUs than the team expected. What is the most likely cause?

questions.explanation: quantizedFlat and diskANN need at least 1,000 indexed vectors for their quantization to be accurate, and below that Cosmos DB runs a full scan, which raises the RU charge. The 50,000 figure is guidance on when diskANN outperforms quantizedFlat rather than a switch-on point, vector search isn't supported at all on shared-throughput accounts, and diskANN works with the cosine distance function, as the Learn quickstarts show.

questions.prompt: A Python team wants to react to inserts and updates in a container, with checkpoints and load balancing across instances handled for them. What should they use?

A Cosmos DB trigger that reads in all versions and deletes mode

questions.explanation: The Functions trigger for Cosmos DB runs the change feed processor on your behalf, keeps its state in a lease container and spreads the work across function instances, and its default latest version mode is available in every Functions language. The processor library itself ships for .NET and Java only, the pull model leaves checkpoints and splitting the feed to your own code, and the trigger's all versions and deletes mode is limited to the .NET isolated worker.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about a container's change feed in latest version mode are true? Select TWO.

options.text: An item created and then updated between reads appears once, in its updated form
Each intermediate update of an item stays in the feed
Deletes can be caught by setting a soft-delete flag and a TTL
The feed can be filtered by operation type, such as updates
The account needs continuous backup to read in this mode

questions.explanation: Latest version mode keeps the current version of each created or updated item, so a create followed by an update before the next read shows up once. It doesn't record deletes, so Learn suggests marking items with a deleted flag and a TTL, which the feed captures as an update. The mode is on by default, while continuous backup and intermediate versions belong to all versions and deletes mode, and the feed can't be filtered by operation type.

questions.prompt: A Python worker reads a container's change feed with query_items_change_feed, and after a restart it must carry on from the last change it processed. What should it do?

options.text: Read the feed ranges again and start each range from Now
Call query_items_change_feed with start_time="Beginning" each time
Let the SDK checkpoint each batch into a lease container
Save the etag continuation token and pass it back as continuation

questions.explanation: In the pull model the continuation token, taken from the etag response header, is the bookmark: passing it as continuation resumes right after the last processed change and takes precedence over any start time. Starting from the beginning replays every change, starting each range from Now skips whatever changed while the worker was down, and lease containers belong to the change feed processor, which Python doesn't have and whose leases can't be converted to continuation tokens.

questions.prompt: A script signs in to PostgreSQL as a developer's Entra user and reuses the password it got at startup; about an hour later, opening further sessions fails authentication. What should you change?

Get a new token for each new connection from one reused credential
Turn off password authentication so the server refreshes tokens

questions.explanation: Entra user tokens for PostgreSQL last about an hour, and the token serves as the password, so a token obtained at startup stops working for new connections once it expires. Asking one long-lived credential for a token per new connection lets the SDK cache and renew it, as the quickstart advises. Rereading the same stored token doesn't renew it, and neither the password-authentication setting nor the administrator role changes how long a token lasts.

questions.prompt: A chunks table will store text-embedding-ada-002 output and needs an HNSW index on it. Which column definition should you use?

embedding real[]
embedding vector
embedding vector(1024)

questions.explanation: text-embedding-ada-002 returns 1,536 dimensions, and a pgvector column has to declare a dimension count that matches the model before it can be indexed. A vector column without dimensions fails index creation with a column-does-not-have-dimensions error, real[] is a plain array that must be cast to vector before pgvector can compare it, and 1,024 dimensions don't match what the model returns.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to add vector search to a new database on flexible server so that the index builds as fast as possible.

options.text: Bulk-load the rows with COPY
Create the chunks table with its vector column
Run CREATE EXTENSION vector in the database
Create the HNSW index on the vector column
Add vector to the azure.extensions server parameter

questions.explanation: An extension must be allowlisted in azure.extensions before CREATE EXTENSION can install it in a database, and the vector type has to exist before a table can declare a vector column. Learn advises loading data before indexing it, because the build is faster and the resulting layout is better, so the HNSW index comes after the COPY load.

questions.prompt: An ingestion job re-embeds revised chunks and must update the stored vector when a chunk's id already exists, or insert the row when it doesn't. Which statement fits?

options.text: UPDATE chunks SET embedding = %s WHERE chunk_id = %s for each revised chunk
INSERT with ON CONFLICT (chunk_id) DO NOTHING so that duplicate ids are skipped
INSERT with ON CONFLICT (chunk_id) DO UPDATE SET embedding = EXCLUDED.embedding
COPY chunks (chunk_id, embedding) FROM STDIN WITH (FORMAT BINARY) for each batch

questions.explanation: ON CONFLICT on the key column turns one INSERT into an upsert: new ids are inserted, and with DO UPDATE an existing row's embedding is overwritten by the value proposed in EXCLUDED. DO NOTHING keeps the stale vector, a plain UPDATE never adds chunks that are new, and COPY is the bulk-load path, listed separately from upserts, that doesn't resolve key conflicts.

questions.prompt: A team stores 3,072-dimension embeddings in a vector(3072) column, and CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw fails. Which change keeps an HNSW index using only generally available features that Learn documents for flexible server?

options.text: Reduce the vectors to 2,000 dimensions or fewer and store those
Create the index WITH (m = 64) so it can hold 3,072 dimensions
Build an IVFFlat index instead, which has no dimension limit
Declare the column as vector so the index ignores dimensions

questions.explanation: For the vector type, HNSW and IVFFlat indexes accept up to 2,000 dimensions, and Learn's flexible-server guidance for larger columns, which can be stored but not indexed, is to reduce their dimensionality. The pgvector project also indexes up to 4,000 dimensions through halfvec half-precision vectors or half-precision indexing, but Learn's flexible-server pages don't document that, which the stem rules out, and DiskANN's higher-dimension support relies on product quantization, which is preview. The m option sets graph connections rather than the dimension cap, IVFFlat has the same 2,000-dimension limit, and a column without a dimension count can't be indexed at all.

questions.prompt: A nearest-neighbour query that ranks rows with the <=> operator shows a sequential scan in EXPLAIN, although an HNSW index built with vector_l2_ops exists. What should you do?

options.text: SET enable_seqscan TO OFF and keep the index
Rewrite the ORDER BY to use the <#> operator
Rebuild the HNSW index with vector_cosine_ops
Raise hnsw.ef_search to 200 so the scan visits more vectors

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL considers a vector index only when its operator class matches the query's operator: <=> is cosine distance and needs vector_cosine_ops, whereas vector_l2_ops serves <->. ef_search tunes an HNSW index that's already in use, <#> would need vector_ip_ops, and discouraging sequential scans can't make the planner use an index that doesn't serve the operator.

questions.prompt: Match each description to the pgvector indexing option.

options.text: No vector index
HNSW
B-tree index on the filter column
IVFFlat
DiskANN

Layered graph that a search enters at a sparse top layer and narrows down to the densest layer
Graph index from a separate extension that depends on vector, aimed at billion-point scale
Exact search with perfect recall, at the cost of scanning every row

questions.explanation: IVFFlat groups the rows into k-means lists and, at query time, probes the lists whose centres are closest to the query, while HNSW builds a layered graph that a search enters at the top and narrows layer by layer. DiskANN comes from the pg_diskann extension, which needs vector, and targets very large datasets, and with no vector index pgvector runs an exact search. A B-tree on a filter column narrows the rows exactly without scanning all of them, so it fits none of the descriptions.

questions.prompt: A table holds 600,000 embeddings, and you create an IVFFlat index with the starting lists value that Learn suggests. What lists value should you use? Answer in lists. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: For tables of up to 1 million rows Learn's starting point is lists = rows / 1000, so 600,000 rows give 600 lists; beyond a million rows it switches to the square root of the row count. The matching starting point for probes is lists / 10, which would be 60 here.

questions.prompt: With pg_diskann, a filtered query that asks for 200 rows stops at 100 in one session, and results must stay in exact distance order. What should that session set?

options.text: SET LOCAL enable_seqscan TO OFF
SET diskann.iterative_search TO 'strict_order'
SET diskann.l_value_is TO 20
SET diskann.iterative_search TO 'relaxed_order'

questions.explanation: A cap at 100 rows is what pg_diskann does when iterative search is off: it fetches l_value_is candidates, 100 by default, in a single step, so a query can't return more rows than that whatever its LIMIT. strict_order keeps searching the graph in batches until the LIMIT is met and returns rows sorted by distance, while the default relaxed_order may return them slightly out of order. A lower l_value_is shrinks the candidate list further, and discouraging sequential scans doesn't lift the cap.

questions.prompt: A 20 GB HNSW index has to be held entirely in the server's buffers under steady production load, and the server is limited to 4 vCores. Which compute tier fits?

options.text: General Purpose
Burstable
General Purpose with Premium SSD v2 storage
Memory Optimized

questions.explanation: Memory Optimized gives 6.75 to 9.5 GiB of memory per vCore, and its 4-vCore sizes have 32 GiB, room for the index, and Learn positions the tier for workloads that need in-memory performance. General Purpose gives 4 GiB per vCore, 16 GiB at 4 vCores, and Premium SSD v2 raises IOPS and throughput but adds no memory; the 4-vCore Burstable size also has 16 GiB and runs on CPU credits that sustained load drains.

questions.prompt: Building a DiskANN index over 5 million vectors on flexible server is slow. Which TWO changes speed up the build? Select TWO.

options.text: Raise maintenance_work_mem for the session that builds the index
Rebuild with REINDEX CONCURRENTLY so it runs in the background
Move the server to the Burstable tier during the build
Set parallel_workers on the table and allow parallel maintenance workers
Lower diskann.l_value_is before running CREATE INDEX

questions.explanation: pg_diskann builds faster with more maintenance_work_mem, and Learn suggests scaling memory up for the build and back down afterwards; parallel workers, set through the table's parallel_workers storage parameter and allowed by max_parallel_maintenance_workers and related settings, also shorten it. Burstable has less compute to give, l_value_is only affects index scans at query time, and REINDEX rebuilds the same index without making the build any faster.

questions.prompt: A flexible server on Premium SSD has 256 GiB of storage and storage autogrow enabled. What size does the storage grow to when autogrow triggers? Answer in GiB. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: On Premium SSD, autogrow always doubles the provisioned size, which also doubles the storage cost, so 256 GiB becomes 512 GiB; Premium SSD v2 grows in finer steps. Storage can't be scaled down afterwards, and the online grow stops at the 4,096 GiB disk boundary, which needs a manual, offline scale.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam's chunks table has an HNSW index on its embedding column, and a query that filters on tenant_id and ranks chunks by cosine distance asks for five; small tenants often get one or two while large tenants get five. What should you change?

options.text: List-partition the table on tenant_id so each partition gets its own index
Rebuild the HNSW index with a larger ef_construction value
Lower hnsw.ef_search on each tenant's connection so the index answers sooner
Normalize the vectors and move the table's index and query to inner product

questions.explanation: With an approximate index the WHERE filter is applied after the index scan, so a shared HNSW index returns about ef_search candidates (40 by default) and a small tenant's few matches among them are what's left after filtering. The pgvector project recommends list partitioning or separate tables for tenant isolation, which gives each tenant its own index and recall, and Learn shows that partitioned tables can be indexed. A smaller ef_search returns even fewer candidates, and inner product or a better-built graph still filters after the scan.

The ::vector cast turns the query embedding that psycopg passes as a parameter into a vector value that pgvector's distance operators accept, which a plain real[] array or jsonb isn't. LIMIT caps the rows, as every Learn example does, whereas OFFSET 5 skips the five closest chunks and TABLESAMPLE belongs after a table name in FROM, where it samples rows at random.

questions.prompt: A RAG endpoint retrieves the top chunks from PostgreSQL and calls a chat model, but answers still include facts that aren't in the manuals. What should the prompt to the model contain?

options.text: The chunks' embedding vectors, which keep their meaning more precisely than text
Every chunk above the similarity cutoff, so the model has the widest context
The retrieved chunks merged into one summary, with source labels removed
Retrieved chunks labelled by source, with an instruction to stay within them

questions.explanation: RAG adds the retrieved text to the prompt as grounding data, and Learn's remedy when grounded answers still drift is clear instructions to stick to that content, plus source labels so the answer can cite it. Passing every chunk above a cutoff spends tokens without telling the model how to use them, a merged summary drops the labels that make citations possible, and embedding vectors carry no readable content for the model.

questions.prompt: Stored chunks were vectorized with text-embedding-ada-002, while the API now vectorizes incoming questions with text-embedding-3-small; queries run without errors, but retrieval quality drops. What should you do?

options.text: Normalize each question embedding to length 1 before comparing it
Rebuild the HNSW index over the chunks so that it adapts to the new model
Embed questions with the same model as the chunks, or re-embed them all
Switch from <=> to <#>, which suits the newer model

questions.explanation: Embeddings from different models live in different vector spaces, so Learn's guidance is to use one embedding model consistently for a vector index, with matching dimensions and distance metric; a matching dimension count only hides the mismatch. Rebuilding the index or normalizing the query vector leaves the two spaces incompatible, and a different operator doesn't make vectors from different models comparable.

questions.prompt: During imports a Flex Consumption function app scales to 60 instances, and the General Purpose server starts refusing connections with too many clients. What should you do first?

options.text: Use the built-in PgBouncer on port 6432 with a small pool per instance
Run a PgBouncer sidecar container next to each function instance's code
Raise max_connections well above the default and then restart the server
Move the server to Burstable, whose built-in pooling absorbs the bursts

questions.explanation: PgBouncer holds a server connection only while a transaction or query is active, so pointing each instance at port 6432 with a small pool keeps 60 instances within the server's limits, and Learn recommends this over raising max_connections, which costs memory as connections become active and needs a restart. Learn's pooling guidance lists sidecars for container platforms, not Functions, and 60 sidecars with their own pools would still multiply server connections, while Burstable servers can't use the built-in PgBouncer at all.

questions.prompt: For each statement about connection limits on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

Scaling the server to a larger compute size leaves its max_connections value unchanged.
Idle connections use no server resources until they run a query.
Applications can use the whole max_connections value, because no connection slots are reserved.

questions.explanation: max_connections gets its default from the compute size chosen at provisioning and isn't recalculated when the compute changes, so Learn advises adjusting it yourself, and a changed value needs a restart. Every connection, idle or active, takes server resources, and the service keeps reserved slots, currently 15, for replication and monitoring, so user connections are fewer than max_connections.

questions.prompt: An app runs 2,000 AKS pods, each with its own PgBouncer sidecar, and the PostgreSQL server runs short of connections. Which change fits?

options.text: Give each sidecar a larger pool size so that its clients wait less
Switch each sidecar's pool mode from transaction to session
Run one central PgBouncer service in the cluster instead of sidecars
Add a second PgBouncer sidecar to each pod to spread the load

questions.explanation: Learn warns that a sidecar per pod multiplies the connections the server sees, so large AKS deployments with hundreds of pods should run PgBouncer as a standalone service that pools for all of them, at the cost of an extra network hop. Bigger pools or a second sidecar per pod add even more server connections, and session pooling keeps a server connection for each client's whole session.

questions.prompt: A profile service uses cache-aside with a 5-minute TTL, and after editing their profile, users keep seeing the old value for minutes. What should the update path do?

options.text: Switch the eviction policy to allkeys-lru

Delete the cached key, then write to the database
Write to the database, then delete the cached key

questions.explanation: Cache-aside invalidates on write: update the data store first and then remove the cached item, so the next read loads the new value. Removing the key first leaves a window in which another reader can load the old row and put it back in the cache, a longer TTL keeps stale data around longer, and eviction only removes keys under memory pressure.

questions.prompt: For each statement about expiration in Azure Managed Redis, select Yes or No.

Yes

A key with a TTL takes no more memory than the same key without one.
The TTL command sets how many seconds a key may live.

questions.explanation: Azure Managed Redis defaults to volatile-lru, so only keys that carry a TTL can be evicted, and EXPIREAT sets expiry at a chosen date and time, whereas EXPIRE counts seconds. Expiration tracking adds memory for each key that has a TTL, and the TTL command only reports how long a key has left.

questions.prompt: A 60 GB Azure Managed Redis cache must work with a client library that doesn't support the Redis Cluster API. Which clustering policy should you choose?

Non-clustered
Active geo-replication

OSS needs a cluster-aware client that connects to each shard, Non-clustered applies only to caches of 25 GB or less, and active geo-replication is a replication feature rather than a clustering policy.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of a cache-aside read in order for an app that caches product records in Azure Managed Redis and, on a miss, caches the record before returning it.

On a miss, read the product from the database
Return the product to the caller
Store the product in the cache with an expiration time

questions.explanation: Cache-aside loads data on demand: the app checks the cache first, goes to the data store only on a miss, adds the item to the cache and then returns it, as the stem requires. Setting an expiration when the item is stored limits how long it can go stale if another process changes the record.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam is creating a 40 GB Azure Managed Redis instance for its semantic cache. Which TWO settings must be chosen at creation for vector search to work? Select TWO.

Enable the RediSearch module

The Well-Architected guidance also requires the NoEviction eviction policy for RediSearch. Flash Optimized doesn't offer RediSearch, TimeSeries isn't needed for vectors, and data persistence is an optional recovery feature rather than a vector search requirement.

questions.prompt: A multitenant API's semantic cache returns an answer cached for one tenant to a user of another tenant who asked a similar question. Which TWO changes each stop this? Select TWO.

options.text: Store a tenant field with each entry and filter lookups on it
Lower the ttl so that a tenant's cached answers expire within a minute
Rebuild the cache's vector index as HNSW instead of FLAT
Give each tenant its own cache index
Raise distance_threshold so that fewer prompts count as a match

Raising distance_threshold loosens matching, because lower values are stricter, a shorter TTL only narrows the window in which the leak can happen, and the index type changes search speed and precision, not who can see an entry.

questions.prompt: Messages with a malformed payload disappear from a payments queue after about ten failed processing attempts, and no code dead-letters them. Where are they now?

options.text: In the queue's dead-letter subqueue, with reason MaxDeliveryCountExceeded
Discarded by duplicate detection, which drops repeated deliveries
Removed for good, because Service Bus deletes messages it can't deliver
In the queue's transfer dead-letter queue, waiting to be forwarded

questions.explanation: Each failed peek-lock delivery raises the message's delivery count, and once the count passes the queue's maximum, 10 by default, Service Bus moves the message to the queue's dead-letter subqueue and records MaxDeliveryCountExceeded as the reason. Nothing cleans that subqueue up, so the messages wait there until someone receives and completes them. The transfer dead-letter queue holds only messages that auto-forwarding couldn't pass on, and duplicate detection looks at resent MessageIds, not at repeated deliveries.

After a transient failure, abandon_message makes the message receivable again at once; defer_message would park it until someone asks for it by sequence number. The dead-letter subqueue is opened by passing sub_queue=ServiceBusSubQueue.DEAD_LETTER to get_queue_receiver; receive_mode picks peek-lock or receive-and-delete, and session_id targets a session.

questions.prompt: A worker needs about eight minutes per message, the queue's lock duration is already at its maximum, and some messages are processed twice. What should you do?

options.text: Enable sessions on the queue so that a single receiver owns each message

Register each message with AutoLockRenewer until the worker settles it
Turn on duplicate detection for the queue that the worker reads

questions.explanation: The lock lasts at most five minutes, so an eight-minute job outlives it, the message becomes visible again and a second worker takes it; AutoLockRenewer (or calls to renew_message_lock) keeps extending the lock until the message is completed. Receive-and-delete removes the message on receipt, so a crash mid-job loses it. Duplicate detection only drops resends that carry a known MessageId, and sessions give a receiver an exclusive session lock that also expires and must be renewed, so they don't stop the redelivery.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the Service Bus feature that meets it.

options.text: Receive-and-delete mode
Scheduled messages
Message sessions
SQL filter rule
Duplicate detection

Ignore a resend that carries the same MessageId within 10 minutes
Make a reminder message appear in the queue 24 hours from now
Give one subscription only the messages whose amount property exceeds 1000

questions.explanation: Sessions give one receiver an exclusive lock on all messages with a session ID, which keeps their processing in order. Duplicate detection remembers MessageIds for a window that defaults to 10 minutes, scheduling (schedule_messages or scheduled_enqueue_time_utc) holds a message back until its enqueue time, and a SQL filter can compare a property with a relational operator. Receive-and-delete only changes how a message is settled, so it meets none of these needs.

questions.prompt: You added a filter rule for high-priority messages to a topic's alerts subscription, but the subscription still gets every message. What's the most likely cause?

Its $Default rule, a true filter, selects all messages
Priority is in the message body, and filters ignore the body

questions.explanation: A new subscription starts with a default rule, named $Default in Learn's filter examples, whose true filter selects everything, and a message enters the subscription when any rule matches, so the new rule changes nothing until $Default is removed. Filters never read the body, but a misplaced property would make the new rule match nothing, which can't explain receiving every message. Sessions play no part in filtering, and rules without actions are combined with OR rather than skipped.

questions.prompt: Which TWO events increase the delivery count of a message received in peek-lock mode? Select TWO.

options.text: The sender sends a copy with the same MessageId
Another client reads the message with peek_messages
The receiver abandons the message
The receiver completes the message
The lock expires before the receiver settles the message

questions.explanation: The delivery count goes up whenever a peek-locked message is abandoned or its lock runs out, and it is this count that eventually sends a poison message to the dead-letter queue. Completing removes the message, a resend with a known MessageId is a new send that duplicate detection may drop, and peek_messages takes no lock, so a peeked message isn't delivered under peek-lock and can't be settled.

questions.prompt: During a burst, some upload jobs wait in the documents queue longer than their time to live and then vanish, so operators can't inspect them. What should Contoso change?

options.text: Turn on sessions for the documents queue

Enable dead-lettering on message expiration
Enable duplicate detection on the documents queue

questions.explanation: With the expiration option off, Service Bus simply drops messages whose time to live has passed; turning it on moves them to the dead-letter queue with the reason TTLExpiredException, which keeps them available for investigation as Contoso requires. Sessions group related messages for ordered handling and still let expired messages be dropped, the lock duration only matters once a receiver holds a message, and duplicate detection drops resends.

questions.prompt: For each statement about Service Bus tiers, sessions and dead-letter queues, select Yes or No.

questions.explanation: Topics and subscriptions need the Standard or Premium tier, and a dead-letter queue supports the normal receive operations, peek-lock and receive-and-delete included. Once sessions are enabled, every message sent to the queue must carry a session ID, and session state can be as large as one message: 256 KB on Standard and 100 MB on Premium.

questions.prompt: A subscription must receive only messages whose region property is EU and whose tier property is gold, with the least effect on throughput. Which filter should you use?

A filter that reads both values from the JSON body

questions.explanation: A correlation filter matches property values by equality and combines several conditions with AND, and Learn advises choosing it over SQL filters because it is much cheaper to evaluate. The SQL filter would select the same messages, but SQL rules lower throughput at the subscription, topic and namespace level. A rule action changes properties rather than selecting messages, and no filter can read the body.

questions.prompt: Python code must read the messages that the audit subscription of the orders topic receives. Which call creates the receiver?

Swapping the two names points at a topic called audit that doesn't exist, a subscription isn't a queue that get_queue_receiver can open by its name, and get_topic_sender only sends messages to the topic.

questions.prompt: You create an event subscription on an Event Grid custom topic (basic tier, push delivery) and keep the default retry policy. What is the policy's maximum number of delivery attempts? Answer in attempts. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: The retry policy of such a subscription allows 1 to 30 attempts, with 30 as the default, next to an event time to live of 1 to 1,440 minutes that defaults to 1,440 (24 hours). You can lower either value when you create the subscription, for example with --max-delivery-attempts in the Azure CLI, and Event Grid namespace topics have delivery settings of their own.

questions.prompt: An event subscription on an Event Grid custom topic has no dead-letter location, and its webhook answers an event with 400 Bad Request. What happens to that event?

options.text: Event Grid drops it without retrying
Event Grid keeps it until the webhook returns 200 OK
Event Grid retries it until the event's time to live runs out
Event Grid stores it in the topic's built-in dead-letter queue

questions.explanation: A 400 (like 413, and 401 or 403 from a webhook) tells Event Grid that delivery can never succeed, so the event isn't retried: it is dead-lettered if a location is set and dropped otherwise. The retry schedule applies to other failures such as timeouts or 503, there is no built-in dead-letter store because dead-lettering is off until you name a blob container, and Event Grid doesn't hold events indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Match each routing need to the event subscription filter that meets it.

Only events whose data.weightKg is above 20

questions.explanation: Event type filtering lists the types a subscription wants, subject filters match the start or end of the subject (for blob events, a container path or a file extension), and advanced filters compare fields in the event data, such as NumberGreaterThan for a numeric threshold. IsNullOrUndefined only tests whether a key is missing or null, and the retry policy controls delivery, not which events are routed.

questions.prompt: An Event Grid custom topic subscription has a 30-minute event time to live and 20 maximum delivery attempts, and its webhook is down for two hours. When does Event Grid stop trying to deliver an event?

When the webhook is back, as retries go on until delivery succeeds
After the 20th attempt, however long it takes

questions.explanation: Event Grid ends delivery at whichever retry-policy limit is reached first, and its backoff schedule (10 seconds, 30 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes, 10 minutes, 30 minutes and so on) fits only about six attempts into 30 minutes, so the time to live wins and a higher attempt count changes nothing. An endpoint that doesn't respond is retried, since only codes such as 400 or 413 stop retries at once, and the policy never extends delivery past its limits.

questions.prompt: Each new blob in a storage account must start three independent handlers within seconds. What should you set up?

A queue gives each message to only one competing consumer, so three handlers on one queue would split the work instead of each seeing every blob; a timer adds up to a minute of delay on every pass, and client-written messages miss blobs uploaded by other paths.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam's ingestion webhook gets no ManualPublished events: its event subscription uses the Event Grid schema, and creating it reported a failed validation. What should the webhook do?

A 202 isn't accepted as a validation response, self-signed certificates aren't supported, and CloudEvents delivery still needs a handshake, an HTTP OPTIONS exchange.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about CloudEvents v1.0 on Event Grid basic-tier custom and system topics are true? Select TWO.

questions.prompt: A timer-triggered function must run at 07:30 UTC from Monday to Friday. Which schedule expression should it use?

questions.prompt: An HTTP-triggered summary function can run for up to ten minutes, and callers get HTTP 502 after about four minutes although the plan allows 30-minute runs. What should you change?

A longer timeout or another plan leaves the 230-second limit in place, and concurrency doesn't shorten one request.

Stacking two trigger decorators on one function isn't valid, Service Bus offers a trigger and an output binding but no input binding, and a timer trigger can't serve HTTP requests.

questions.prompt: A function app works locally but fails in Azure because INVENTORY_API_URL is missing; the value is in the Values section of local.settings.json. What should you do?

Shipping or committing the file doesn't help, because the app in Azure doesn't read it (and Learn says never to store it in a remote repository), and a restart only reloads the existing app settings.

questions.prompt: A new Python API must reach a database that only accepts traffic from a virtual network, and it should cost nothing for compute while no requests arrive. Which hosting plan should you choose?

questions.prompt: A Python function app needs system libraries that you can supply only in your own container image, using generally available hosting only. Which option fits?

questions.prompt: In one region, a pay-as-you-go subscription runs only Flex Consumption apps on 4,096 MB instances, with the default regional quota and maximum instance counts that don't limit them. How many of these instances can run at the same time? Answer in instances. Enter a number.

questions.prompt: A function must rotate a secret automatically some time before the secret's expiration date. Which Key Vault event type should its Event Grid subscription filter on?
